item.title: Conductor is joining Meta
item.description:
I have big news: Conductor is joining Meta.

We launched Conductor a lifetime ago, in the distant past of July 2025. Writing most of your code with agents (let alone a team of coding agents) felt crazy back then. You trusted us to come along for the ride, and we cannot thank you enough!

We have some big, crazy plans for the next interface. If you liked Conductor, you’re gonna love what’s coming. We’ll have something new for you to use early next year.

Conductor will keep working as normal till then, except for Conductor Cloud, which will shut down over the next few weeks. We’ve built an easy way to transfer Conductor Cloud workspaces to local, and we’re around to help make the transition as easy as possible. Reach out to [email protected] if you need anything.

Thank you again for your support!

Charlie

item.title: Have I befriended a murderer?
item.description:
Thoughtful stories for thoughtless times.

Longreads has published hundreds of original stories—personal essays, reported features, reading lists, and more—and more than 14,000 editor’s picks. And they’re all funded by readers like you. Become a member today.

Edward Abel Smith | Longreads | November 3, 2026 | 5,962 words (21 minutes)

On a sunny Saturday morning earlier this year, I was driving my two daughters to the playground through patchy phone signal when a voicemail notification appeared. Pressing play impatiently, an upbeat voice with a north of England accent bellowed through the car’s loudspeaker: “Hi Ed. I’ve just been flicking through The Times, and I’ve seen you’ve been chosen as their book of the week. Bloody well done, my friend! I am super proud.”

I was stunned. My book, A Hateful Decision, about Churchill’s attack on the French navy during the Second World War, had just been published. Being named The Times Book of the Week was, without question, the highlight of my writing career. But the way this news was delivered felt profoundly weird. The man who had congratulated me—referring to me as his “friend” with such sincerity—was Robin Garbutt, and he’d called from Wealstun Prison, where he was, and still is, serving a life sentence for the murder of his wife, Diana. She was killed in her bed, beaten so brutally that her face was barely recognizable by the time the police got there.

In 2021, I was researching a possible sequel to my first book, a biography of Ian Fleming, the creator of James Bond. While at the National Archives in West London, partly through a filing error and partly through my own boredom, I found myself looking at recent criminal case files rather than the wartime naval intelligence records I had come for. One caught my eye immediately: Diana Garbutt, a woman murdered in the flat above the post office she ran with her husband Robin in the North Yorkshire village of Melsonby.

The only available document for her murder was the judge’s summing up, and it was damning. Robin had called the emergency services on the morning of March 23, 2010, saying their post office had been robbed at gunpoint. After the perpetrators left, he claimed he had run upstairs to find Diana dead. But no one in the village had seen any evidence of the robbery, even though it was a busy morning. The paramedics who first attended Diana noted that she had rigor mortis—a sign she had died many hours before Robin claimed the robbery took place. It appeared Robin had invented the robbery to cover his own murderous tracks. The descriptions of the wounds she had sustained in her final moments of life were horrific. As I read on, I felt nothing but contempt for her husband. The judge made it clear to the jury that he believed Robin to be a killer. Ten of the 12 jurors agreed, and Robin was found guilty by a majority verdict.

When I got home from the archives, I looked up the case online, curious to know what had become of Robin. There was a strange sense of relief to learn he was still behind bars. But as I scanned through the search results, something made me double-take: a website dedicated to Robin Garbutt. What kind of convicted murderer has his own website? It turned out his family had set one up, maintaining throughout that he was innocent of killing his wife. I was, of course, skeptical; a lot of people in prison claim they should never have been convicted. But what struck me about Robin’s website was the list of supporters: family, childhood friends, and a remarkable number of Melsonby residents, a village of fewer than 800 people.

Getting in touch with Robin was surprisingly straightforward. The “contact us” section of his website directed me to his friend Jane Metcalfe—a proud woman from the same part of the country as Robin, and someone who would rather use ten words when one would suffice. She was desperate for more media attention for the case. A new author was hardly what she had in mind, but she graciously stuck with me, suggesting I write to Robin directly. We started to exchange letters through a system called eMates. I would type a letter to Robin, which would be printed and delivered to his cell. For an extra 26 pence, I could include a response sheet, on which he would write a reply by hand.

Over the next six months of writing to each other, Robin would instruct Jane to send me documents from his case. I started to build up my own archive of police reports, trial transcripts, and witness statements, all arriving in hard copy through the post. Thanks to years of reading and watching fictional detectives like Sherlock Holmes and Miss Marple, a surprising amount of the prosecution documents made sense to me. But there was one element I still couldn’t understand: What type of person could murder their wife in such a merciless way? For someone painted as so gentle by those who knew him, it just did not add up. Perhaps he was a psychopath? That possibility scared me the most. At the same time, I was desperate to find out more—to the point I thought I might scrap Ian Fleming and write a book about the murder instead.

When I broached the topic with Robin in one of my many letters to him, he suggested we should meet. I jumped at the chance, due to curiosity as much as anything else. As far as I was aware, I had never met a convicted murderer. I had certainly never set foot in a prison. As a director in a large corporation, it was a far cry from the air-conditioned London offices I was used to.

Jane was instrumental in the coordination, kindly collecting me from York Station, where she brushed aside my outstretched hand in favor of a warm bear hug. The half-hour drive to Wealstun Prison was conducted at such speed I was no longer frightened by the prospect of entering a high-security prison so much as making it there in one piece. Jane did not look at the road nearly as much as I would have liked, either, but in fairness maybe she did not need to—she had made this journey so many times before. Her red Ford Fiesta told its own story: a flyer tucked in the windscreen declaring Robin’s conviction the country’s worst miscarriage of justice, the back seat buried under the paperwork of his various appeals. By the time we pulled up outside the prison, I had been given the full case for Robin’s innocence at considerable volume. Then Jane drove off and left me alone in front of a great fence that seemed to swallow the sky.

Visiting a prison for the first time is not unlike catching a flight. There are the same queues, the same searches, the same surrendering of your belongings, the same slow procession through a series of checkpoints, each one deeper into the complex than the last. Eventually, I was shown into the visiting room—a vast, gymnasium-sized space of plastic chairs and laminate tables, with a small canteen in one corner and a children’s play area in the other. I bought two cheese toasties and two coffees and sat down to wait.

When Robin walked in, my first thought was how little he matched what I had expected. He was tall and trim, calm in a way that seemed entirely unperformed. The man who had been photographed entering court looking gaunt and hollow-eyed had filled out; more than a decade of prison routine seemed, paradoxically, to have done him good.

He sat down, thanked me for the sandwich and drink, let me flounder through some small talk about the weather, and then, with the patience of someone who has had a great deal of practice at waiting, he broke in gently. “If you write a book about me,” he said, “it’s important that you feel you can ask me anything, even if it might seem really insensitive. You need to make up your own mind about who you think killed Diana. I’ll tell you the facts. Anything you want to know, I will tell you. But I won’t try to persuade you either way.”

It was a disarming thing to say. I noticed, as he spoke, that he twisted the wedding ring on his finger—slowly, almost unconsciously, as though it were a habit he was no longer aware of.

I liked Robin immediately. He was warm, he put me at ease, and there was a tiredness about him—heavy bags under his eyes, a particular quality of sadness—that felt, even then, at odds with the version of him the prosecution had described. But underneath the warmth of the visit was a thought I couldn’t quite shake: that this was precisely how a guilty man would want to come across. There was an uneasy feeling that I was being played. I wrote in my notebook on the train back to London, “Can I imagine R standing over his wife’s bed with a metal pole, brutally beating her to death while she slept?”

After my first visit, Robin began calling me. Usually once a week, at lunchtime, when he and his fellow inmates were locked in their cells, a quiet hour that became, for both of us, a kind of fixed point in the week.

He had only been at Wealstun for a few months when we first made contact. Before that, he had spent over a decade at HMP Frankland, one of Britain’s highest-security prisons, nicknamed “Monster Mansion.” Wealstun brought an important change: a telephone in his cell, rather than a queue for the communal phones. For Robin, it meant a small measure of privacy. For me, it meant he could call any day. If I missed a call, he couldn’t try again for another hour, and I had no way of calling him back. So whenever his number appeared on my screen, I stopped whatever I was doing and answered. I found myself ducking into storerooms, or stepping out of meetings with a vague excuse, or pressing the phone to my ear in empty corridors while colleagues walked past, entirely unaware of who I was talking to.

Our conversations had a rough structure. We would begin with pleasantries—how the week had been, what we had each been doing. And it was here, every time, that I would catch myself. I found myself talking down my own life: glossing over a weekend away, understating the dinner with friends, mentioning my newborn daughter only briefly and moving on. Because on the other end of the line was a man who had spent the weekend sitting in a cell. There is no natural way to bridge that distance. Instead, I minimized it, which came across as guarded and standoffish. But despite my awkwardness, Robin always stayed interested in my life; I found myself touched.

We would then move on to his case. Robin’s life is consumed by the process of trying to overturn his conviction through an arduous, complicated, and deeply flawed system that moves at a snail’s pace. I had never heard of the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) before I started speaking to Robin. It is now a body I could lecture on at length, should anyone be foolish enough to listen. In brief, the CCRC is an independent organization that screens claims of miscarriage of justice, deciding which cases merit referral to the Court of Appeal and which are rejected before they can get there. Robin refers to his dealings with the CCRC as a game of Whac-A-Mole: Each time a prosecution pillar is addressed, the CCRC pulls up another point to dismiss his application.

The motive the police gave for Diana’s murder was financial: Robin had been stealing from the Post Office and murdered his wife when she found out, inventing the robbery to cover both the killing and the missing money. But when Robin first applied to the CCRC in 2015, he pointed out that Post Office records for the six years he had worked there—which the Post Office had previously failed to disclose—showed that the spending patterns the prosecution used to indicate theft were entirely normal for their branch throughout his and Diana’s tenure. The CCRC accepted this was significant. They rejected the application anyway.

My own research into their finances has done little to simplify the picture. The Garbutts lived on the premises of their business, making it almost impossible to draw a clean line between personal and company expenditure. By all accounts, they were just getting by, though with some exceptions: over £5,000 spent on weekend retreats, a holiday to America, and tickets to Glastonbury. Such expenses weren’t impossible on their income, but they sat uneasily against the broader picture of a couple living hand to mouth. What impressed me when discussing this with Robin was his ability to never come across as bitter toward those who implicated him. His arguments were never personal against anyone—even though he was accusing them of causing his wrongful conviction.

The fraud motive still never quite added up, especially when I considered a separate scandal surrounding the Post Office’s Horizon computer system. In 2019, investigations and a campaign by a handful of wrongfully convicted individuals revealed a huge miscarriage of justice: hundreds of subpostmasters in Britain wrongly prosecuted for financial discrepancies caused by faulty Horizon software—the same software used to generate the financial records for Robin’s post office. I am not suggesting Horizon exonerates Robin. But it raises the possibility that the prosecution’s motive is built on data from deeply unreliable software. For me, that’s important.

Robin applied to the CCRC again in 2017, this time targeting the question of opportunity. The expert who analyzed Diana’s stomach contents had placed Diana’s time of death between 2:30 a.m. and 4:30 a.m.—a window that made Robin the only person who could have killed her. But Robin’s legal team argued to the CCRC that an independent pathologist found this expert’s methodology to be flawed.

This timeline had other issues, too. Robin had been running the village shop within his post office branch since 4:30 a.m. on the morning of the murder—supposedly with his dead wife upstairs—serving a steady stream of around 70 locals and commuters from Scotch Corner, one of the busiest junctions in the north of England. David Harper, the milkman, was among the first, arriving at around 5:15 a.m. “I had a nice chat with Robin as I always would,” he recalled. “He was his usual friendly, affable, and personable self.” At around 6:45 a.m., Robin’s friend Brian Hird came in for his copy of The Northern Echo. “He was just his normal cheery self,” Brian told me. As Brian was paying, he heard something from behind the counter. “It sounded like a woman’s voice coming from the stairs behind the shop,” he explained in Robin’s trial. “I think she just said one word, ‘Robin.’ I was sure it had come from their apartment.” If Brian was right, then Diana was alive at 6:45 a.m.—over an hour and a half after the prosecution’s suggested window closed. For reasons that have never been fully explained, the jury did not accept his account. Robin has never understood why. Brian remains a friend and still sometimes visits Robin in prison, along with dozens of others who have stood by him all these years.

But if Diana was not killed before 4:30 a.m., when did she die? I have spent much of the last five years obsessing over 79 seconds. That is the window between the post office safe being remotely unlocked at 8:35:54 a.m. on March 23, 2010, and Robin’s 999 emergency call being received at 8:37:13 a.m. In that time, according to Robin, a man in a balaclava appeared, pointed a gun at him, and said, “Don’t do anything stupid. We have your wife.” Robin then had to bolt the front door, fill a holdall bag from the safe and the till, let the robber leave through the back, run upstairs to find Diana, and call the emergency services.

I have put the timeline to investigators, criminologists, and former police officers. The broad consensus is that it was possible, but only just. Measuring the dimensions of the shop to the stairs and up to the bedroom, I have recreated the steps at home several times, and in the allotted time. But “if Robin had killed her,” one of his friends from the village asked me, “why would he have given himself such a short window of time?” It is the same kind of question I hear time and again, no matter which side of the argument someone is on. If they believe Robin is guilty, then they say, “That does not make sense; he is lying.” And if they believe Robin is innocent, then they say, “Robin would make up something more believable to cover his tracks.” For me, 79 seconds is tight. But it is not impossible, and impossibility is the only thing that would have settled it for me.

The CCRC accepted that the initial pathologist’s evidence should be removed from the prosecution case. They rejected Robin’s application anyway.

The third CCRC application, submitted in 2019, added grounds related to the murder weapon. The pole used to beat Diana to death was found on a wall near the post office a few days after the crime. But footage from a local television crew, time-stamped from the day after the murder, showed that the wall was empty—meaning the pole could not have been placed there by Robin on the night of the murder, as the prosecution had claimed. DNA analysis also revealed that the officer who had spotted the murder weapon had left his DNA not only on the bar itself, but at the crime scene, in a property he maintained he had never entered. None of Robin’s DNA was found on the murder weapon. The CCRC accepted these points. The application was rejected anyway.

It has been suggested to me that there was something nefarious going on with the policeman whose DNA was discovered at the scene. He was on holiday for the week of the murder, but he decided to return to work several days early, at which point he found the murder weapon. He didn’t explain his premature return. And he could not recollect what he had been doing at the time of the murder. No alibi. No attempt at an alibi. My efforts to track him down for an explanation, or to obtain a comment from North Yorkshire Police, have so far been unsuccessful.

But having learned so much about this case, I feel the DNA can be explained by simple incompetence. There is plenty of evidence for that. The judge in Robin’s trial described North Yorkshire Police’s investigation as having a “regrettable lack of professionalism.” When investigators compared crime scene photographs taken on the day of the murder to ones taken afterward, they noticed discrepancies: bedside table lamps that had mysteriously disappeared, later found to have been moved to the back of the wardrobe. A clump of hair on the bed—matching neither Robin’s short gray nor Diana’s dark brown—bagged as evidence, then subsequently lost. An investigation riddled with errors like these is also one where a police officer’s DNA ending up on a murder weapon is, at least, explicable.

Until learning all this, I had been working from a position of skepticism about Robin’s innocence, looking for reasons to doubt the verdict. I soon found myself doing the opposite: looking for reasons to trust the investigation. I struggled to find them.

By the time I first met him, Robin was working on his fourth CCRC application with his pro bono legal team. He described it as his “last chance,” although I wondered whether he had said the same about the previous three. At the time of writing, that application has been sitting with the CCRC for two years. Every three months, Robin receives an update letter. Each one contains a variation of the same sentence: that his case officer is “familiarising myself with the issues in your case.” Robin will often talk very calmly, in a measured way, about the CCRC, and end with the same sentence: “Anyway, sorry to rant, Ed.”

Something kept catching, like a loose thread. I did not trust the investigation. But the CCRC might still know something I did not—with their unfettered access to police databases, internal memos, and forensic evidence. A flawed institution is not automatically a wrong one.

After his fourth application was submitted, I did something I had been avoiding for a long time. I put it to Robin directly: Perhaps the CCRC, for all its faults, had looked at the full picture and reached the right conclusion. That perhaps he was guilty. That perhaps he had murdered his wife. I had been dancing around the question since the moment I first walked into Wealstun Prison. Asking it out loud felt like a betrayal—of the connection we had built, of the hours he had given me, of the trust he had extended to a stranger. But I also knew that if I never asked it, I would always wonder.

The disappointment in his voice surprised me, not because I expected him to react any differently, but because it was the first time he had not been his deliberately optimistic self.

“Ah, um,” he stuttered, then breathed out heavily. “I don’t really know what to say,” he continued, so obviously deflated.

“Do you mind me mentioning it?” I asked, as the silence on the other end of the phone started to unnerve me.

“No, gosh, no,” Robin replied, seemingly snapping out of his melancholy. “It is the waiting for news,” he added matter-of-factly. “The fear and dread that they are going to deliver another nail in the coffin. It is exhausting. The stress is something to add to the bucket of pain.”

Whenever I finished my conversations with Robin, I usually returned to whatever I’d been doing—another mind-numbing meeting, an overly complex spreadsheet, a pointless conference call. But after this one, I needed time to reflect. His reaction stayed with me. Robin had always struck me as emotionally consistent: calm, friendly, and honest. Hearing the dissatisfaction in his voice when I suggested the CCRC could be right was unnerving. It must have been a double sucker punch: I was questioning his innocence while defending the institution he blamed for keeping him locked up so long.

What surprised me most was my own reaction. I was genuinely worried I’d upset Robin—not that he might stop talking to me, ending my plans for a book, but that he could be sitting in his cell, sadly pinching the bridge of his nose the way he did when I’d met him, because of me. It was the first moment I realized Robin might be becoming more than the subject of my research. He might be becoming a friend. And I wasn’t only troubled by having upset him. Robin hadn’t actually answered my question; the one that suggested he might be guilty.

The following week, Robin didn’t call. It wasn’t unheard of for him to miss a week: Despite prison life seemingly leaving him to watch time pass, he actually had a job running admissions as lorryloads of young men arrived each week. Phone calls were also expensive, and sometimes he simply couldn’t afford one. But with no way to reach him, a nagging feeling took hold that he was upset with me.

Another week later, an A5 envelope arrived in the post. On the back, in tiny writing: Robin Garbutt and his seven-digit prisoner number. I could feel there was something inside besides the card. With excitement, I tore it open.

Ed,

I’m very conscious that you have very little paperwork on my case, despite everything Jane has sent. Anyhow, when at Frankland, I applied for and was given a laptop solely for my case—on it was tonnes of paperwork, legal letters, CCRC stuff plus a PDF file of all my solicitor’s correspondence. This file will show you the layout of the house and post office, there are no horrific scenes of Di, but some distressing ones of blood—so not nice. When I left Frankland they put all that onto a ‘dongle’ which is enclosed. It is my only one (!!) so we will want it back in your own time—no rush at all.

That’s me Ed. Take great care and speak soon.

Many thanks,

Robin

It took months to wade through what was on the stick. The material was vast: witness statements; unused evidence; legal correspondence; letters Robin had sent to lawyers, forensic experts, and private investigators around the world, begging for help and, in most cases, receiving no reply. Reading them was quietly devastating.

There were also spreadsheets he had meticulously compiled: “Timeline for Moor Road and the Shop 6.30 to 8.30” runs 240 rows deep, cataloguing every witness’s recollection from the morning of the murder, each one cross-referenced to a statement number. I pictured Robin in his cell in the small hours, tapping away on his laptop while over 800 fellow inmates slept around him.

What struck me first was not what was in the files. It was the fact that he had sent them at all. I had just confronted him with the possibility that he was guilty—the most direct challenge I had put to him in months of conversation. His response was not to go quiet, not to cut me off, not to become defensive or combative. He had flooded me with everything he had. His only copy. A man with nothing to hide, or a man who had calculated, very precisely, that transparency was his best remaining move. I genuinely could not tell which.

Among the files were some truly fascinating nuggets, some of which made me question the case in its entirety. Buried in one of the tedious police reports was a reference to the discovery of underwear found at the top of the contents in Robin and Diana’s outside bin, stained with what appeared to be rust, consistent with that found on the murder weapon. Apart from that paragraph, it was not mentioned again. It took considerable searching before I found a witness statement, taken from one of Robin’s neighbors more than six months after the murder. “I have also today been shown some pictures of a pair of grey Calvin Klein boxer shorts, which were labelled as exhibit KC8. I can say that I have boxer shorts like this. I think that I had two pairs and when I checked today, I only have one pair left.” This piece of evidence was never explored further, and the underwear was never tested to establish whether the brown substance was rust from the murder weapon.

Then there was a Crimestoppers report stating that a man who lived nearby had been seen with a firearm and a large amount of cash the day after the murder, boasting that he had “bashed her around the head.” What was most interesting was the timing. I have not been able to establish exactly when the tip was submitted, but several days passed after the murder before police released details of how Diana had been killed. Had this tip come in before that information was made public, it could be very significant. I have since tracked down the person named in the report. His address, age, and name match a man currently serving a lengthy sentence for trying to rob a safe in a shop in Manchester, 100 miles from Melsonby, with an imitation firearm. He has not responded to my attempt to contact him.

These were the first credible alternatives I had come across. I was now not just considering whether Robin might not have murdered Diana—I was looking at other suspects. But the nature of Diana’s murder gave me pause. It seemed personal. The ruthlessness of the beating she sustained while she slept pointed to someone who knew her. Someone who resented her. Not a stranger.

I had been sitting with that thought for some time when a name began to crop up in witness statements from Diana’s family and school friends: her stepfather. The statements referred to her troubled relationship with him and alleged that she had sustained sexual abuse at his hands throughout her childhood, which had never been reported. In the months before her murder, however, she had apparently told members of her family that she had finally built up the courage to go to the police. Her stepfather has since died, so the full truth may never be known.

Each of these threads complicated the picture further without resolving it. I had begun with one question—Did Robin kill Diana?—and ended up with several more, each pointing in a different direction.

Around this time, I started working with a production company on a documentary that would become “Murder at the Post Office,” a three-part television series for Sky. The question of how to frame Robin on screen was one I avoided as long as possible. In print, ambiguity is easier to sustain; you can hold two possibilities open simultaneously and let the reader sit with the tension. Television is less forgiving. Producers want a direction. I found myself in conversations about whether Robin should be presented as likely innocent, contested, or unknown—and I realized I genuinely did not know which category I believed he belonged in. I settled on contested. It felt the most honest. Robin watched the documentary when it aired. He called me the following week. He was grateful, he said. He thought it was fair. I was relieved, then immediately suspicious of my own relief. Why did his approval matter to me? I was supposed to be a journalist, not his advocate.

I still regularly make the eight-hour round trip from my home in the South of England up to Yorkshire to see Robin. I spend more time with him than many of my other friends. Each visit reminds me of the power of face-to-face conversation in a world that is moving increasingly online. Being able to look Robin in the eye as he answers a question gives me a perspective no phone call can replicate. Since the awkwardness of suggesting he could actually be guilty, I have felt freer to challenge him when we are together, to ask the questions that have been nagging at me. Was his marriage to Diana as happy as he makes out? From speaking to some people who still live in Melsonby, I had heard rumors of Diana seeking comfort elsewhere. Robin was quick to dismiss this. “Every marriage goes through difficulties, Ed,” he said calmly. “We had our tough patches, but we were happier than ever by the time she was taken from us.”

One of the unexpected consequences of spending five years on this case has been getting to know Diana. Not literally, of course; I never met her. But through her letters, her photographs, the testimonies of her family and friends, a person has gradually come into focus. A woman who, like all of us, was imperfect, but also deeply loyal, loving, and by all accounts great fun. The more I have learned about her, the more I have felt a responsibility toward her. Whatever the truth turns out to be—whether it was Robin who killed her, or someone else entirely—Diana deserves better than to remain a footnote in someone else’s story. That feeling has kept me going on the days when the case has felt too complicated, too unresolvable, and too consuming to continue with.

It also makes me wary of Robin. The what-ifs constantly circle. The question I find myself asking is no longer simply whether Robin is innocent or guilty, but whether he is the person who killed Diana. It has become personal. When I sit across from Robin in the visiting room, listening to him talk about her with what seems genuine tenderness, I cannot always hold those two things together: the man in front of me and what was done to her. Yet some days the contradiction is easy to set aside, and it is just a husband sitting across from me, eager to talk about his wife. Robin will dig deep into the back of his mind for seemingly mundane moments from their past. The time they could not find the car keys. When she found his hidden stash of biscuits. The dinner party they hosted in fancy dress. Although I have so many questions circling in my mind about their respective lives, one thing I am certain of is how much Robin loved Diana. Whether he killed her in a fit of rage or not, there is no question that he worshipped her.

I have recently allowed myself to lean toward a belief in Robin’s innocence, or at least toward a version of events in which the truth is considerably more complicated than the one a jury was asked to believe. I haven’t concluded, of course; I am not sure I will ever conclude.

Five years ago, I believed I could read people. I prided myself on it. It is, after all, a useful quality in business: the ability to size someone up quickly, to sense when you are being told what you want to hear. I assumed that five years of phone calls and prison visits, of watching Robin answer difficult questions, of learning when he deflects and when his tone changes, would have sharpened that instinct further. Instead, the opposite has happened. All our time together has— unintentionally—created a relationship, and my vision is clouded. I find myself second-guessing judgments I would once have made instinctively at work, with my friends and even my family. There is always a small voice now, asking whether I am simply a bad judge of character who got lucky, or unlucky, with Robin. Because the truth is that he is the only person on the planet who knows what happened in that bedroom to Diana.

My current relationship with Robin is still confusing. Our conversations are not like my conversations with other friends. I am still restrained. We rarely talk about films, or sport, or what we did at the weekend in any sustained way; when we do, those exchanges feel slightly performative on both sides, as though we are both trying to prove to the other, and perhaps to ourselves, that this is a normal relationship. It is not. The case is always underneath everything, even though I am yet to write that book. I have not found the right angle to tell Diana’s story.

But over time, I have, gradually, found myself opening up a little more to Robin. When my second child was born at the start of 2022, among the well wishes that arrived at our home was a card he had sent. According to the British justice system, one of the oldest and most revered on the planet, it was a card from a murderer. And yet here he was, sharing the moment with me, becoming in some small way part of my life alongside my family, my closest friends, my colleagues.

I have become more conscious of this recently. Whenever Robin calls, I still try to answer. Often it will be over the weekend, when I am with my family.

On one crisp, bright morning, I was in the garden speaking to Robin while trying to play hide-and-seek with my two daughters.

“Daddy, who are you speaking to?” my eldest asked.

“Robin,” I replied, apologizing down the phone, embarrassed by our opposing situations.

“Is he your friend?” she asked, with a child’s complete innocence. She looked at me for an answer. On the other end of the phone, Robin waited too, silent.

“Yes, darling,” I replied. What else could I say?

Edward Abel Smith is an author, producer, and investigative journalist. His work has covered some of the UK’s most serious claims of miscarriages of justice, including his multimillion-downloaded podcast about convicted nurse serial killer Lucy Letby, Was There Ever A Crime. His latest book, Murders in the Dark (DK, March 2027), reopens the case of the 1942 London Blackout Ripper and reveals new evidence that the wrong man may have gone to the gallows.

item.title: Show HN: After a decade of reversing, I got co-op working in DOS Wing Commander
item.description:
An 11 year journey to play DOS Wing Commander together

By danielrh

When we were kids, my brother Patrick and I would steer our space fighter with one of us on controls and the other on the lasers and afterburner boost. We always dreamed of playing the Wing Commander series cooperatively as wingmates rather than as a two headed hydra in a single craft.

In the beginning we were searching for where we were

On October 4, 2015 as I was playing the classic Wing Commander in Dosbox I realized the whole memory probably fit in that 640K Bill Gates apocryphally said “ought to be enough for anybody”. If I could dump the memory and identify the locations that held the X,Y,Z coords for the player & wingman we could let the network packets control the wingman.

The actual quote

“I have to say that in 1981, making those decisions, I felt like I was providing enough freedom for 10 years. That is, a move from 64 K to 640 K felt like something that would last a great deal of time. Well, it didn't.” Source

This presented a clear problem to attack: out of fewer than a million bytes how would we identify that location? I decided to simplify the problem by trying to empty the game of other entities. A stopped player shouldn’t change coordinates. We could snapshot the memory twice when stopped to identify “background” memory churn. Then burst forward and measure again. If we didn’t turn (mouse was disabled) we might only change one axis. The next problem was to find an empty region of space. We had to start without our wingman Paladin, since he would move with us. After a miserable mission, letting the nefarious space cats overwhelm Paladin and running back to the spacecraft carrier, the Claw, the next mission was primed for a flight through empty space. I launched and flew directly ahead until everything despawned and took the memory snapshots using the DOSBox MEMDUMPBIN debug-command.

Now I had to discover anything that had not changed between the memory snapshots where my star fighter was in the original position but things that had changed when my star fighter moved.

(snapshotorigin ⊙ snapshotlater) ∧ (snapshotorigin ⊕ snapshotmoved)

There were 35 distinct clusters of bytes that changed in the data segment. By inspecting these visually and looking for floats or small integer changes when I moved, I narrowed it down to a dozen locations it could be. I went to the chase camera view as well, and this helped to narrow it down to 13D3:A9C2. I had the DOSBox debugger add integers at that address with its SM command and that caused the ship to jolt forward to a new location.

CAE2, since thre were three 32 bit ints that zeroed out when the craft was stopped.

I had fun driving my ship around with the memory editor and reproduced it around the Claw and other NPC ships.

Then we searched for what we faced

I set it down for nearly a year but in September 2016 I decided to write a small tool to automatically compare DOSBox snapshots instead of using the vbindiff GUI only. Directionality turned out to be more difficult so I set down the problem for a few more months and picked it back up in November.

To find the memory location of the rotation, I needed to look harder. As it happened the vectors were made of 4 byte scalars with 256 as 1.0 and valid positive vector positions between 0 and 255. This meant that most small rotations only changed a single byte. However, fortune was smiling on me that day because of what appeared to be a programmer joke at the time. Wing Commander reserved 64 slots for entity properties. In hex this would span numbers from 0x00 to 0x3F. However the programmers decided to use 0x3F for temporary usages and place the camera in 0x3D. Since 3D graphics were still nascent, the programmers may have thought it a good laugh to write 0x3D every time they needed to manipulate the 3D camera. That put a temporary variable two slots from the camera variable. And up and forward were also next to one another. This gave a nice wide region where I could locate those single byte changes. The first byte I understood was the y of the right vector; the print window I put around it happened to cover the camera's copy of up, which is where the overwrite experiment started. Furthermore, I rolled the ship over, and tripped sign extension, which caused all 3 adjacent bytes to switch from 0x00 to 0xff. Between these two facts, I noticed the temporary and camera bytes in the hex dumps. Writing to them did not help, since they were overwritten every frame, but luckily I wrote some extra bytes to the next vector as well, which was forward[0]. This caused a noticeable shift in the starfield and meant that I could now start investigating the code.

I put memory watchpoints on the addresses and traced the vector-add function called by the per-ship physics function called by a per-frame function and eventually the main loop.

It was now time to locate the byte sequences in IDA and start annotating the game. Wing Commander Multiplayer was now just a matter of repeating these techniques and figuring out how to puppeteer one ship from another's input.

Then we searched for how to act

December 2016 had shattered my illusion that we would be able to drive Wing Commander with writes to global memory alone. The details of manifesting laser fire or heat seekers were far too complicated to puppeteer solely from the addresses. We would need to co-opt the very functions in the original game to get the most accurate experience. One initial thought was to “will” the program counter to the right place, but we would need a way to insert arguments and return back from whence we came. Moreover, many of the functions were in various overlays that required indirection to invoke. It appears that Borland had a different overlay per compilation unit (C++ file) and they were dynamically loaded in different locations depending on the path the player took beforehand.

Patrick and I had to figure out a good trampoline system to call functions with the correct arguments. We chose the “Loading WING COMMANDER” string at 13D3:0187 and eventually 13D3:0395 “Sorry, an error has occured while %s”[sic] to hold the trampoline.

We would have DOSBox push CS:IP to the stack, then relocate the instruction pointer to the string above.

00 terminates any string pointing here. pushf; pusha the game is mid-frame; leave registers as we found them xor si,si; push si argument: ship 0. Later thunks use mov si,imm16 for each argument call far 12D7:0156 through the stub, so it works wherever the overlay is loaded pop si; popa; popf cdecl: caller cleans the arguments retf back to the CS:IP DOSBox pushed

We noted with joy that this caused the laser cannons to activate.

In March of 2017, we found a predictable location in the main loop (0560:20E3) to hook so we would not need to worry about being in an unpredictable part of the game, and in July we located the do_damage function and prevented the game from calling it as the secondary player.

Then we tried to bring together fields from afar

In August of 2017, we authored the networking protocol which was a simple TCP client/server architecture with protobuf game messages. Every frame every ship's position would be sent from the leader plus fire events, despawning and damages. The client would reply with its own position, if any lasers were fired or if some cataclysmic event had happened (ejection, landed, died).

Each player would have their own craft as entity 0 and the other player as entity 1, which required a swap when receiving packets from the other emulator.

These packets modified memory directly or were added to a job queue of events that had to happen that frame.

We started with a very simple trampoline:

pushf pusha nop popa popf retf

When Borland's overlay loader swaps a code page in, it walks the chain of saved BP frames on the stack and patches any return address that points into an overlay. The hand-made stub had no frame, so the walk read garbage and the game died at random moments. This was a constant thorn in our side from October to December.

The fix was to make the trampoline look like a Borland function:

push bp mov bp, sp nop (0x90) ; welcome to the 0x90's pop bp retf

We configured DOSBox to notice when the program counter reached the nop and instead inject its call from the job queue of things that should happen. The job queue was based on what was necessary to make the game function correctly in a multiplayer scenario.

In October 2017 we noticed that ephemeral objects would be located in different slots for different players. Having the new hook from DOSBox also let us determine when the function had returned, so we could note down which numeric slot a new ship or projectile had been spawned into.

Ephemeral objects had their own spawn rules and could occupy shared areas of the 61 entity slots. We modified the location that ephemeral objects were placed in so we could confine them to slots 12 to 15 and keep multiplayer locations consistent.

In December we decided to change the client to store a mapping of server ship IDs to local IDs, so we could stop forcing the spawn function return. This allowed packets to translate between local and host IDs. Finally asteroids started to work in multiplayer.

In 2018 we focused on animating explosions, missiles, and autopilot.

The search continued for both success and defeat

In June of 2019 we noted the mission victory calculation was flaky and finicky. We decided to conduct a binary search to find the location of the actual victory point tally. We copied the entire 64K data segment across the network, and slowly cut it in half. After many bisections, we located 80 bytes at 13D3:D248 which held the mission tree. And in October we found the overall victory point counter at 13D3:C280 and mission numbers at 13D3:C255 and C256, which allowed us to select the mission to play from a dropdown, years later.

And finally the joy of combined words

In early 2020, we identified the function that played comm text. This allowed us to send chat over the network and hook typed chat directly into the system so it played using the wingman's VDU. It allowed a very immersive way to chat that reminded us of some of the frenetic sequences in the game.

Some final work in 2020 left the game in a playable state, but we were out of ideas on how to actually share the fun with friends. Expecting people to locate a copy of that old game, compile or download a strange version of DOSBox, share each other's public IPs and punch the firewalls and play together was sadly a bridge too far.

We had a few family playthroughs but the game rested on GitHub, mostly idle.

And in 2026, machine assisted development helped us laugh together

Until now. With the advent of widespread WebRTC, robust emscripten support, and a new system we put together called lobbylink, the time seemed right to revive the project and share it more widely.

lobbylink

I built https://github.com/danielrh/lobbylink which is a simple golang lobby system, depending only on a websocket library, that orchestrates peer to peer WebRTC connections. It can run on any small server and simply allows players to connect to one another using WebRTC and a shared room code. The server has a static allowlist of origins and can let browsers or client software in almost any language connect to it with a room code. The room code is used to locate other players with the same room code and they get notified of all joiners in that room. The server also runs coturn and mints TURN credentials in its joined reply, so players behind restrictive firewalls can join.

I ported over the transport to lobbylink and asked an LLM to configure the build scripts to target emscripten and take a GOG Inno Setup installer package of Wing Commander and unzip it and use it as data files for emscripten. The combination of these makes it possible to download Wing Commander from GOG, drag and drop it into the client-side browser storage, enter a room code, and play.

The game is playable at https://fireflyk64.github.io/dosbox/ and the emulator is at https://github.com/danielrh/wcmulti.

And as an added bonus I asked an LLM to add voice chat as well for realtime voice in game using a second WebRTC peer connection to carry audio, if people choose. And so we can fly and laugh together.

item.title: Ripple-65B Preview: U.S. Open-Weight SOTA on Agentic Coding
item.description:
Introducing Ripple-65B Preview,a Frontier Open-Weight Model

Ricursive Intelligence is a full-stack artificial intelligence lab building self-improving systems by co-optimizing hardware, software, and model.

To power our chip design platform, we trained a language model from scratch that sets a new U.S. open-weight SOTA on agentic coding. We optimized the model architecture for our training and serving platforms, driving substantial efficiency gains.

Today, we release Ripple-65B Preview, a general-purpose variant of the proprietary model that powers our AI chip design platform. The model is pretrained on 12 trillion tokens with support for up to 1M context length. Ripple-65B Preview delivers strong results on agentic coding, achieving U.S. open-weight state-of-the-art (80.52) on TerminalBench 2.1 and surpassing significantly larger US open-weight models such as Reflection Beam 501B (80.1), Meta Muse Spark Open 816B (76.4), Thinking Machines Inkling 975B (63.8), and NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B (56.4).

Rippleâs dense model architecture provides strong reasoning performance with low-latency token generation. The modelâs small parameter envelope also enables it to run efficiently on local devices such as NVIDIA DGX Spark, which feature high compute FLOPs with low memory bandwidth relative to datacenter accelerators.

Ripple-65B Preview is available on Hugging Face, Together AI, GMI Cloud, and OpenRouter. Fireworks goes live later today.

Achieving U.S. Open-Weight Frontier at One-Tenth Cost

LLM pretraining is legendarily expensive. In 2023, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said that GPT-4 training costs exceeded $100 million. In the following year, Dario Amodei said that frontier AI models can cost up to $1 billion to train, projecting that costs would rise to $10-100B by 2026 to 2027 for pretraining alone.

In contrast, we developed and trained Ripple-65B Preview for only $32M, which is one-tenth the cost of the previous open-weight SOTA on agentic coding, as estimated to the best of our knowledge.Â¹ Note that $32M is our full R&D cost starting from scratch, including pretraining ladder development, data mixing, evals, debugging, synthetic data generation, posttraining recipe development, and the final hero pretraining and posttraining run.

Steep Ascent Reinforcement Learning

Rather than investing in a brute-force RL climb, we carefully iterated on our SFT and RL recipes with a focus on compute efficiency. We opted not to buy any posttraining data, instead devising our own synthetic data pipelines, quality filtering, and coverage metrics.

Our mixed RL recipe uses truncated importance sampling, score centering, and linear length penalty with high-quality long-horizon synthetic environments. The RL tasks are tuned for our model capabilities, and we continuously added harder tasks as the model improved.The end result was a steep RL climb from a strong initial SFT checkpoint. We reached a TerminalBench 2.1 score of 80.5 with only 1.4M rollouts, roughly 70x fewer rollouts than Reflection Beam, the prior SOTA.

A Co-Designed Model Architecture

Ripple-65B Previewâs architecture was designed to be trained and served efficiently on NVIDIA hardware. A key objective was to make design decisions which reduce pretraining and posttraining infrastructure complexity while still enabling strong reasoning and agentic performance. Therefore, we chose to train a modernized dense Transformer model rather than use Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) like other labs. This decision quickly paid off, and we were able to train a strong model from scratch while maintaining a solid MFU (40%) throughout pretraining and posttraining, even with simple sharding, no custom kernels, and no quantization.

Ripple-65B Preview uses a thin-and-deep model aspect ratio, with a narrow d_model (5120) and 80 total layers. To improve reasoning performance, we overprovision the number of attention heads while increasing the SWA-to-global layer ratio and reducing SWA window size to compensate for the increased cost. In addition, we added FFN activation clipping, gated attention, global NoPE, and value residuals.

Careful Model Laddering Led to Large Improvements

We optimized Rippleâs pretraining recipe through a series of careful model laddering experiments.

Our starting point was Olmo 3âs model ladder, from which we tested interventions at small scale with a focus on improving coding capabilities. Our v1.0 ladder implemented StepFun batch size and learning rate scaling laws, and v1.1 implemented our new ladder which smoothly scales architectural dimensions and model depth. Ladder v1.2 switched from the post-norm baseline to pre+post norm, which was neutral at small scale but showed improvements starting at 4B. Ladder v1.3 implemented sigmoid gated attention. Ladder v1.4 (2-stream mHC) showed good results at smaller scale but did not improve at 4B scale, and was therefore rejected. Ladder v1.5 switched to global NoPE and added a final LR cooldown to zero, and ladder v1.6 added value residuals. In the final version, we switched to our custom pretraining dataset with substantially upsampled code.

Together, the compounded changes improved compute efficiency on code as measured by dolma_stack CE by up to 16x at 4B model scale. In other words, our final Ripple model ladder can be used to achieve similar code performance to the Olmo 3 ladder with 16x less compute. Note that the slope of the Olmo 3 ladder baseline is shallower than ladder v1.0+, which shows that the compute efficiency improvement will increase with additional scale.

Conclusion

We built Ripple-65B Preview to begin closing the loop between models and the hardware that fuels them. An internal variant of this model powers our AI chip design platform, and we look forward to seeing the capabilities that emerge as we scale toward the frontier.

We were fortunate to build on top of existing open-source contributions, including those from the Olmo team at the Allen Institute for AI (AI2), Prime Intellect, RadixArk, and NVIDIA. A strong open-source ecosystem is also self-improving, where contributors strengthen the ecosystem, which in turn draws more contributors.

At Ricursive, we are selectively hiring exceptional researchers and engineers as we push the frontier of full-stack AI from model to silicon. If youâre interested, check out https://www.ricursive.com/careers.

Â¹ U.S. open-weight players like Reflection were reported to commit to $150M per month for compute at SpaceX Colossus to train their models. Reflection reported that Beam took 4 weeks to pretrain and 4 weeks to posttrain.

item.title: Insects don't swarm at LED lights
item.description:
3 November 2026

Remember when you used to encounter swarms of insects around outdoor electric lights? Their well known attraction to outdoor lights is used by entomologists and moth lovers to conduct insect surveys. All you need is a light and a white sheet to see who’s flying at night.

Nowadays, if you want to attract insects, you have to be picky about the light you use. As everyone changes over to LED lights, we see the color difference but we can’t see the crucial difference in insect attraction between incandescent and LED.

Our guide Roland Rumm on the WINGS Veracruz trip explained what happens with insects in the switch to LED lights. His family has an outdoor dining space that is well lit with artificial light. As a child he loved to watch the geckos climb to the lights and eat the insects. (This gecko can change to a bland gray color when he needs to.)

In recent years the family changed over to LED lights and the geckos disappeared. Were the geckos gone? No. But far fewer insects were attracted to the LED lights so the geckos had no reason to show up.

In 2024 the BBC wrote about Why insects are drawn to artificial light at night:

Flying insects use moonlight to navigate. Since the moon is always above them, they orient themselves so that the light shines on their backs. That’s how they stay upright in flight.

Moonlight contains ultraviolet (UV) and infrared wavelengths because it is merely reflected sunlight. Insects cue on UV, believing it to be the moon. When artificial lights transmit UV they look like moonlight so insects orient their backs to it. Consequently they circle the light and even flip upside down when the artificial light is pointing up to the sky!

Incandescent lights transmit UV but LEDs do not. Insects are far less attracted to LED.

In 2016 scientists at the University of Bristol, UK ran experiments to compare insect attraction to four types of light: Incandescent (tungsten filament), Compact fluorescent, “Cool-white” LED and “Warm-white” LED.

We conducted field experiments to compare the relative attractiveness of four commercially available “domestic” lights, one traditional (tungsten filament incandescent) and three modern (compact fluorescent, “cool white” LED and “warm white” LED), to aerial insects, particularly Diptera. We found that LEDs attracted significantly fewer insects than other light sources, but found no significant difference in attraction between the “cool” and “warm white” LEDs. Fewer flies were attracted to LEDs than alternate light sources, including fewer Culicoides midges (Diptera: Ceratopogonidae). Use of LEDs has the potential to mitigate disturbances to wildlife and occurrences of insect?borne diseases relative to competing lighting technologies.

— Experimentally comparing the attractiveness of domestic lights to insects: Do LEDs attract fewer insects than conventional light types?

Here’s what they found. NOTES: CFL = Compact fluorescent, FIL = incandescent (the old lightbulb), LEDC = LED cool white, LEDW = LED warm white light.

Typically LEDs do not emit UV light and are more energy efficient than traditional technologies. Electrical energy is converted almost entirely into electromagnetic (EM) radiation within the range of the visible light spectrum (400–700 nm) and therefore not wasted on producing wavelengths of light invisible to the human eye, that is, UV and infrared (IR). Thus, LEDs are less attractive to many insects than lights which emit UV light.

— Experimentally comparing the attractiveness of domestic lights to insects: Do LEDs attract fewer insects than conventional light types?

So that’s why there are very few bugs circling LED lights at night.

According to the BBC, this trait of LEDs is a good thing because incandescent (UV) artificial light at night distracts insects so much that they don’t reproduce, don’t feed, etc. Thus artificial light is considered a major reason why insect populations have declined. See: The impact of artificial light at night on nocturnal insects: A review and synthesis.

item.title: Show HN: Gauge – Open-Source CLI to recursively improve your docs
item.description:
An open-source CLI for hillclimbing Agent Experience.

Make your Skills, CLIs, SDKs, MCPs and docs easier for coding agents to discover and use. Gauge runs real agents against your product, captures where they get stuck, and lets your own coding agent test fixes before you publish them.

The full loop runs locally with Docker and your existing agent subscriptions or API keys. No Gauge account required.

Website · Documentation · Hosted Gauge · npm · Changelog

Sign in and choose your organization to access Chat data:

gauge auth login gauge orgs use acme gauge chat categories list gauge chat query datasets

Chat commands cover topics, prompts, tags, brands, reports, answers, and citations. See Gauge Chat commands and organization selection and upgrade guidance. These commands use hosted Chat data and do not require Docker.

Gauge runs and analyzes coding sessions to find the issues that coding agents run into.

Common findings include:

An interactive command blocks a coding agent An agent reaches for deprecated commands or outdated API patterns A Skill goes unused even when it should help with the task An agent confidently claims a limitation that does not exist An agent cannot figure out the intended workflow across multiple commands

The right fix might change error messages, Skill content, help text, code, or documentation. The Gauge CLI lets you validate proposed fixes before release.

Gauge is designed to be used by your coding agent. Point it at this repository and ask it to get started, or follow the steps below in the project you want to improve.

You need Node.js 22.13+, npm, Docker running Linux containers, and credentials for the agent you want to test. Gauge supports Claude Code, Codex, Pi, and OpenCode. It can use native Claude/Codex logins or API keys; agent usage is billed through your provider or subscription.

npm install -g @withgauge/cli gauge local runtime pull

Gauge downloads the published Docker image pinned to your CLI release. The image contains the agent harnesses and standard development tools.

From your project directory (Git is optional):

gauge init --local

This creates a private .gauge/ workspace, including a SQLite database and local backend preference. Plain init changes no tracked files. Add --cases when you want shared Markdown cases: it also writes a gauge.json manifest, gauge-cases/, and guidance in AGENTS.md. Commit those shared files. Keep .gauge/ private: it contains durable measurements and analyses.

The Gauge skill teaches your coding agent where to find the CLI's instructions:

gauge install-skill

Hillclimbing means making a change, measuring whether it helped, and repeating.

Define realistic tasks. Your agent saves evals or preference prompts with stable identities, editable defaults, and observable outcomes. Use optional Markdown cases for fully specified measurements intended for sharing or CI. Test your current product. In local mode, Gauge starts fresh Docker sessions and injects the working-tree version of your configured inputs. Each test agent sees the task and configured inputs within its sandbox. Local mode supports Skills, SDKs, CLIs, and files. Hosted compute adds support for docs, authenticated MCPs, and authenticated APIs. Find friction. Gauge normalizes events from Claude Code, Codex, Pi, and OpenCode into consistent transcripts. In local mode, your agent reads the evidence, checks the outcome against the criteria, and identifies what slowed or blocked the task. It publishes structured Findings and judgments through gauge run analysis save. In hosted mode, this analysis happens automatically after each session. gauge run insight shows the evidence. Change and retest. Your agent edits the product or its guidance and reruns the affected cases against the new artifacts. Analyze the evidence. Check whether the original problem disappeared, whether the task succeeded, and whether the change introduced new friction.

Skills and file inputs are read from your working tree. For an npm CLI or SDK, build and pack a new tarball before rerunning. Gauge installs these pre-release artifacts in the test sessions, so you can validate a fix before publishing it.

The CLI handles execution and evidence collection. In local mode, your coding agent authors the changes and analyzes the local results.

Saved evals and preference prompts live in .gauge/gauge.sqlite locally or in your hosted organization. Shared file-based cases optionally live in gauge-cases/; gauge.json declares project inputs and automation. Both measurement sources support local and hosted execution, with the input differences described below. Start with a saved local eval; use a shared case when the task is ready for teammates or CI.

Example: test a release-notes Skill

Create skills/release-notes/SKILL.md:

--- name: release-notes description: Write release notes for a new version in the team's format. --- Write RELEASE-NOTES.md with the version as its title, an Added section for new features, and a Fixed section for bug fixes. Use one bullet per change.

For a fresh project, use this gauge.json:

{ "version": 2, "inputs": { "release-notes": { "type": "skill", "path": "skills/release-notes" } } }

Save the task and criteria:

gauge eval create --local --name "Release notes" \ --agent codex --samples 1 \ --text "Write the release notes for version 1.2.0. We added dark mode and fixed a login crash." \ --criterion "Team format: RELEASE-NOTES.md has a version 1.2.0 title, dark mode under Added, and the login crash fix under Fixed."

Use the returned eval ID to preview, then launch when ready:

gauge run --eval <eval-id> --local --input release-notes --dry-run gauge run --eval <eval-id> --local --input release-notes gauge instructions session-analysis --local

The preview checks local readiness without launching an agent. Your coding agent then reads the session and publishes its analysis. After changing the Skill, rerun the same eval ID: the new batch snapshots the current input files while the baseline remains intact. Keep the task, criteria, and model pin fixed, analyze both batches, then compare:

gauge run --eval <eval-id> --local --input release-notes gauge run compare --local --baseline batch=<before-id> --candidate batch=<after-id>

For a choice study, use gauge preference create --kind open-ended with a task that lets the agent choose its approach, then gauge run --preference <id>. Supplying the Skill measures choice after that exposure, not discovery on the web.

For a shared or automated version of the eval, use the same input configuration and create gauge-cases/release-notes/basic.md:

--- criteria: - name: Release notes follow the team format rubric: RELEASE-NOTES.md has a version 1.2.0 title, dark mode under Added, and the login crash fix under Fixed. config: agents: - agent: CODEX_CLI sampleCount: 1 inputs: [release-notes] --- Write the release notes for version 1.2.0. We added dark mode and fixed a login crash.

This case uses Codex; use CLAUDE_CODE, PI, or OPENCODE to test another harness with its configured credentials. The agent starts in an empty workspace with the Skill installed. The task does not explicitly tell it to use the Skill, so the session also reveals whether it discovers the guidance.

gauge run --verify --local gauge run --dry-run --local gauge run --local gauge run list --local -o json

Verification checks the config and cases. The dry run previews the sessions and checks local runtime and credential readiness. Neither launches an agent.

Results, transcripts, and available diffs stay under .gauge/. Have your coding agent follow gauge instructions session-analysis --local to assess each criterion and report friction with supporting evidence.

After editing the Skill, rerun the case:

gauge run --local --files "gauge-cases/release-notes/*.md" gauge run compare --local --baseline batch=<before-id> --candidate batch=<after-id>

Use the batch IDs printed by the runs. The comparison summarizes completion, available turns/duration, and published criterion judgments. Read the findings and evidence to determine whether the fix worked.

Gauge helps teams improve how AI agents discover, choose, and use their products. Agent Experience measures whether agents can successfully use your product. Agent Preference examines which tools agents choose for a task and why.

This CLI puts that work in the terminal where you and your coding agent already work. Local execution supports the complete evaluate, analyze, fix, and retest loop. The hosted platform adds managed infrastructure and shared measurement over time.

Sign in with gauge auth login to use hosted Chat and Agents. On a remote terminal, use gauge auth login --device. See signing in for help with login and API keys.

Local Hosted Gauge Execution Docker on your machine, using your agent credentials Managed compute; sessions keep running when you close your laptop Results and analysis File evidence; SQLite measurements, judgments, and Findings authored by your coding agent Shared results, automated judging, and tracking over time Queries Run summaries and Findings; supported fields are discoverable Findings and additional reporting datasets Product inputs Skills, npm CLIs and SDKs, docs and files, web fixtures Also native binaries, GitHub-resolved website previews, and authenticated MCPs/APIs Iteration Test working-tree changes and pre-release artifacts Also controlled response rewriting and managed optimization trials Automation CLI scripts and local batches Also scheduled measurements, GitHub App PR checks, and greater concurrency Account No Gauge account Gauge workspace and credits

Web fixtures let you test changes to content an agent encounters, such as a docs page, without publishing them first. They replace pages or route a site to a preview in both local and hosted runs. Hosted Gauge's gateway also brokers credentials and can rewrite responses separately for each session.

Project inputs on saved eval/preference launches, and --dry-run for those saved measurements, are currently local-only. For hosted working-tree input snapshots and previews, use case files or a case spec with gauge run --hosted. For example, the shared case above supports gauge run --hosted --dry-run; hosted previews contact Gauge and may upload inputs. Local and hosted saved measurements have separate IDs and storage.

To move a project to hosted execution:

gauge onboard gauge init --hosted gauge instructions --hosted

gauge onboard signs you in and creates or selects a workspace. gauge init --hosted changes this checkout's private backend preference; it does not move local measurements or history into hosted storage. Hosted runs use workspace credits. See the documentation for hosted setup, PR checks, and optimization workflows.

The CLI bundles instructions for coding agents, so the guidance matches the installed version:

gauge instructions gauge instructions init gauge instructions run gauge instructions eval gauge instructions preference gauge instructions session-analysis gauge instructions --list gauge --help gauge run --help

Use -o json on read commands for scripts and agent analysis. Check the runtime with gauge local runtime inspect; configure provider credentials with gauge local profiles --help. Update the CLI with gauge update.

See the CLI reference for configuration, supported inputs, credentials, background runs, cleanup, and CI usage.

The installed CLI collects command usage by default: command name, timestamp, CLI version, and a random installation ID. It excludes arguments, prompts, file contents, and account identifiers. Disable collection with:

gauge telemetry disable

Or set GAUGE_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1 for a process or CI environment. See telemetry details for storage, delivery, and the distinction from authenticated API usage analytics.

From the repository root:

npm ci npm ci --prefix cli npm run check

check builds, typechecks, runs tests, and verifies packaged installs. It does not require a Gauge account, Docker, a database, or another repository checkout.

Directory Contents cli/ CLI commands, bundled agent instructions, and API schemas packages/local/ Local Docker session runner and runtime Dockerfile packages/agent-adapters/ Agent transports and evidence decoding

For a CLI development loop after building, use npm run dev --prefix cli -- --help.

Docker integration checks run in the custom runtime workflow. The runtime and CLI release workflows validate and publish versioned artifacts. Runtime releases produce a qualified manifest; commit it as cli/runtime-manifest.json before releasing the CLI.

The shared libraries also have public npm releases, published by the agent adapters and local execution workflows from gauge-sh/gauge-cli. Each package's npm trusted publisher must point to that repository and its matching workflow.

See Releasing for repository setup, package permissions, and the runtime-to-CLI release sequence.

Issues are welcome. Forking and building your own version is the preferred way to customize Gauge. Only the Gauge team merges changes into this repository; we periodically consider bringing community changes upstream. See CONTRIBUTING.md.

For account questions or private reports, contact support@withgauge.com.

item.title: Residential proxies detected on White House network
item.description:
Our Residential Proxy Observatory, launched earlier this week, is a first-of-its-kind interface that gives researchers a global view of residential proxy and anonymized internet activity.

While our team was looking through it, we noticed residential proxy exit activity on AS2650. AS2650 is registered to the Executive Office of the President, the federal agency that hosts the White House network. Residential proxy services sell access to everyday devices, letting customers send traffic through them so it appears to come from that device's network.

What we observed

From October 5 to November 3:

Our residential proxy enumeration pipeline exited through the White House network 236 separate times. Those exits came from 6 addresses, on 26 of the 30 days. 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

To make sure this was not a fluke, we checked these addresses against other residential proxy detection services, such as Spur and Synthient. Their public IP context pages independently identify these addresses as residential proxy exits.

This is public access. Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.

Why this is concerning

Most of the activity happens in the evening, Eastern time: about half of it falls between 5 p.m. and midnight, and almost none happens in the early morning. That pattern suggests a person rather than a public guest Wi-Fi network: someone regularly on the White House network late into the evening, whose device is infected with a proxy SDK. Our data shows the exits, not the device or the person behind them.

Past research has shown that poorly secured proxy SDKs can allow internal network access and lateral movement. This is how past botnets have spread. In A Broken System Fueling Botnets, the researchers at Synthient documented how the Kimwolf botnet reached at least 2 million devices, mostly Android devices with an exposed ADB service, through residential proxy networks. If an SDK on this network has the same kind of flaw, anyone buying proxy access could use it to reach internal systems.

No place is too remote

The White House is not the only surprise in the observatory. Residential proxies also reach some of the most isolated places on the planet.

Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha is the South Atlantic territory that includes the most remote inhabited island in the world. We recorded 413 addresses and more than 32,000 observations there, split between Starlink and the island's local internet provider, Sure Saint Helena.

We also recorded three observations from Antarctica. All of them come from a Cloudflare WARP address that points to McMurdo Station.

Other remote places with activity:

Pitcairn: 1 Starlink address, 1 observation. Norfolk Island: 1 Norfolk Telecom address, 4 observations. Svalbard: 1 Starlink address in Longyearbyen, 3 observations. Also seen: the Falklands (388 addresses), the Chagos Islands (43), Tokelau (21) and South Georgia (7).

Residential proxies have infected every corner of the world, and it looks like there is no place they cannot reach. Layer3 Intel tracks residential proxy and anonymization infrastructure worldwide. Even when the proxies hide in networks on the farthest corners of the planet, we can still observe them, leaving threat actors no place to hide.

Death comes for XSLT

Last halloween, Google decided to kill XSLT. That was not a unilateral decision mind you, Google said âjumpâ and other browser vendors said âhow high?â

In response, I published my Intent to Deprecate and Remove Google Chrome. A performative declaration of course, I donât install spyware.

Fearing my parody lacked seriousness, I created XSLT.RIP to ensure the developer world was informed of Googleâs death note. This did the trick, although a few commenters believed it was satire. There is subtlety to XSLT.RIP. The website itself is built with XSLT and when Google kills XSLT theyâll kill my website.

The web standards process and its stewards (Big Browser) used to adhere to a social contract. Backwards compatibility was a major design principle. Under no circumstances do you ever purposefully break the web.

Google decided to renege and break the web.

XSLT.RIP will be broken soon and Iâll sit back and watch Google break it. 17 November 2026 appears to be the date of execution. Some Chromium-based browsers have been running a man-in-the-middle attack by injecting propaganda into XSLT websites.

This site uses XSLT; that functionality is being removed from this browser very soon. When that happens, this page will likely no longer display correctly. You might be able to install a browser extension that allows you to continue viewing it. Otherwise, you should contact the maintainer of the site for further information.

Source: This site uses XSLT: what Chromeâs banner means - XSLT Playground

Iâm testing on ungoogled-chromium so who knows how itâs intended to look.

The line of death is another âsocial contractâ that Google has forgotten. Theyâre blaming website owners and acting like questionable purveyors of free public Wi-Fi. This is arrogant and intrusive.
