item.title: Hacking the Xbox 360 Hypervisor Part 3: Bad Update Improvements
item.description:
Hacking the Xbox 360 Hypervisor Part 3: Bad Update Improvements

Welcome to part 3 of the Hacking the Xbox 360 Hypervisor blog series. In this part I’ll go over what happened after I released the PoC for Bad Update, and how it went from taking ~20 minutes with a ~30% success rate to being near instantaneous with a near 100% success rate. If you haven’t already I highly recommend you read (or at least skim through) part 1 and part 2 as this post will reference a lot of the material discussed there. This part will be very short but will catch you up for part 4 which covers the peer pressure exploit and will be out soon.

Rock Band Blitz

In the months following the release of Bad Update v1.0 there were two major improvements made to it by others. The first by “ihatecompvir” and “InvoxiPlayGames” is a new game save entry point in the demo version of Rock Band Blitz (RBB) called DaTArrest. The demo version of RBB is a package file that’s normally downloaded from the Xbox Live store for free and saved to your console’s HDD or memory unit. When the Xbox 360 got support for using USB sticks as storage devices all of the packages signed to boot from the HDD or memory unit were grandfathered in to also boot from USB storage devices. This means the RBB demo package can be copied to a USB stick as a normal file and launched on any console on a software version that supports it.

By exploiting some memory corruption vulnerabilities in the game’s DLC parsing code they were able to craft a game save file that when loaded would bootstrap the Bad Update stage 2 ROP chain and begin the hypervisor exploit chain. Using RBB as an entry point we no longer needed the Tony Hawk American Wasteland game disc. Running the Bad Update exploit was now as simple as copying some files to a USB stick, plugging it into your console, and launching Rock Band Blitz from the dashboard.

Hypervisor Race Condition Optimizations

Shortly after the RBB entry point was discovered I received a pull request from “Máté” who had made some improvements to the hypervisor race condition part of the exploit. These improvements included a hash table for precomputing and storing the malicious ciphertext values, a better cache flushing primitive, and improved thread scheduling between the XKE payload thread and ciphertext overwrite thread. The combination of these improvements reduced execution time down to a few seconds and the race condition had a much higher success rate.

Ciphertext Hash Table

In part 2 I talked about attacking encrypted memory by using hypervisor APIs to create encrypted memory allocations at predetermined memory addresses and used two different memory pathways to capture the ciphertext for some chosen plaintext data. Using this primitive I was able to craft ciphertext data to get kernel mode code execution as well as the ciphertext data used to attack the LZX decompression code in the bootloader update XKE payload.

The whitening value used in the memory encryption scheme is 12 bits large which gives 1024 unique ciphertext combinations for some given plaintext data. However, in my original PoC I was only generating the ciphertext for one of the 1024 possible whitening values and the reason for that was a two part failure on my end. When I originally prototyped out the ciphertext attack I did actually try using a lookup table for ciphertext combinations but I wasn’t able to get it working.

The first issue was I was using a very old ~2011 era hypervisor/kernel build (it was just what all my old research was based on) which was doing a TLB flush for the encrypted VA range in the hypervisor function that setup the memory encryption. In later hypervisor builds that TLB flush was removed because the kernel wrapper function for this hypervisor function already does a TLB flush for the VA range. However, I call the hypervisor syscall directly (skipping the kernel wrapper code which does the TLB flush) and since the TLB is lazy-loaded the whitening bits would become stale and the resulting ciphertext read out of memory was invalid.

When testing the exploit on the 17559 (latest) version hypervisor the lookup table was causing issues and rather than investigate I decided I’d fix it later and moved on. By the time I got to the end of the exploit I had become so blinded by tunnel vision chasing CPU cache issues that I had convinced myself the lookup table just wasn’t going to work. What I should have probably done (aside from investigate the lookup table issues when they surfaced) was to put this project down for a few weeks and come back with a clear mindset. Oh well, lesson learned…

Getting into the implementation details of the hash table, we use the first N bits of the ciphertext we expect to see in memory as an index into two arrays. The first array contains the first 64-bits of the oracle ciphertext which is used for validation in case there’s ever a collision in the hash table. The second array stores our malicious ciphertext we want to write into memory.

// Index bits of the ciphertext lookup pseudo-hashtable

#define HASH_BITS 20

struct CIPHER_TEXT_DATA

In order to make this as efficient as possible (remember we’re racing the CPU and cache here) we ignore collisions. It’s better to have a few collisions and have to skip some iterations on the race condition loop than to implement support for buckets in the hash table. Instead we compensate for collisions by choosing a sufficiently large enough number of bits for the hash table key such that the number of collisions is on the order of single digits, if we even have any (majority of the time there’s 0).

However, more bits in the hash table key means a large array to hold the entries (meaning more memory is used) which could potentially work against us as we’ll be performing more fetches from RAM since CPU cache is being thrashed. Máté’s original PR used a key size of 10 bits but I later upped this to 20 bits which seems to be a happy spot where there’s usually no collisions or if there are it’s a low single digit number. The total size of memory needed to hold both hash tables is about 24MB.

// Scan all 1024 possible whitening bits.

for (int i = 0; i < 1024; i++)

{

// Allocate encrypted memory.

HvxEncryptedReserveAllocation((DWORD)pMemoryAddress, BaseAddrPhys, UpdateDataSize);

// Manually flush the TLB entry for the encrypted allocation address so we pick up the new whitening value.

// trigger to know when to start the race attack.

KeFlushCacheRange(pMemoryAddress, 0x80);

KeFlushCacheRange(pUpdateData + ScratchOffset, 0x80);

// Get the corresponding cipher text for our malicious dec_output_buffer pointer which points to the hypervisor code we want to overwrite.

*(ULONGLONG*)(pMemoryAddress + 0x2B20) = pCipherTextData->dec_end_input_pos;

*(ULONGLONG*)(pMemoryAddress + 0x2B28) = pCipherTextData->dec_output_buffer;

__dcbst(0, (char *) pMemoryAddress + 0x2B00);

KeFlushCacheRange(pMemoryAddress + 0x2B00, 0x80);

KeFlushCacheRange(pUpdateData + ScratchOffset + 0x2B00, 0x80);

// Store cipher text for our malicious dec_output_buffer pointer into the lookup table.

pCipherTextData->ReplacementCipherText1[index] = *(ULONGLONG *) (pUpdateData + ScratchOffset + 0x2B20);

pCipherTextData->ReplacementCipherText2[index] = *(ULONGLONG *) (pUpdateData + ScratchOffset + 0x2B28);

// Free the encrypted allocation.

result = HvxEncryptedReleaseAllocation((DWORD)pMemoryAddress);

}

}

Looking at the snippet above we can see how the hash table is built. We loop 1024 times to exhaust all possible whitening values for this page of memory. Each iteration we encrypt the page (which will increment the whitening value), get the ciphertext for the LZX decoder data we expect to be in memory and the ciphertext for our malicious data, then add them to the hash tables. On lines 15-16 we can see the HvxFlushSingleTb call that thwarted my own attempt at using a hash table, and on lines 30-31 we can see how the first N bits of the expected ciphertext is used as the hash table key.

Improved Cache Flushing

In my original PoC I used a unique feature of the Xbox 360 CPU to lock away half of the available L2 cache to try and put as much pressure on it as I could. The L2 locking technique was pivotal in the original PoC but it didn’t put as much pressure on CPU cache as I would have liked. Putting pressure on CPU cache is particularly annoying because kernel mode (where the exploit code is running) cannot use certain cache flushing instructions due to them being privileged and only usable in hypervisor mode.

Additionally, the hypervisor only runs with CPU caching enabled when operating on encrypted memory which makes finding a hypervisor level cache flush primitive difficult. I tried to work around this by finding a hypervisor syscall that would read a large amount of encrypted memory, and I did find one syscall that fit the description, but it wasn’t nearly enough for what I needed. That function also had locks in it which prevented me from executing it on multiple threads simultaneously.

However, there was a kernel mode cache instruction I completely overlooked that Máté had found to work extremely well, dcbz or data cache block set to zero. Aside from just zero’ing out a CPU cache line this instruction has an interesting side effect:

If the cache block is already in the data cache, all of its bytes are cleared to zero. If it is not in the cache, the block is allocated and initialized directly in the cache to zero without reading the old contents from main memory.

So if this instruction is used on a memory address that’s not currently in CPU cache the CPU will allocate space for it and potentially evict something else to make room for it. By running the dcbz instruction over large regions of memory it can be used as a cache flush primitive and force old data in CPU cache to be evicted. In Máté’s original implementation he allocated an 0x80000 byte region of memory then looped over it and for every 0x80 bytes (the size of a cache line) called dcbz.

This worked extremely well, however, I found that by increasing the allocation size by 3x and calling dcbz at three distinct locations I was able to assert slightly more pressure on CPU cache which would be important for another improvement I’ll get to later on. Here’s the final implementation:

Improved Thread Scheduling

In part 2 I talked about trying to schedule the exploit threads on different hardware threads and how I got the best results by putting them on CPU hardware threads 0 and 1 (which are both on core 0). I don’t really know anything about how CPUs work at a hardware level but I suspected that the load/store memory transactions from both hardware threads on the same core were being queued onto the L2 crossbar in some sort of per-core fashion. Thus by putting the exploit threads on the hardware threads for a single core the writes from the exploit thread and reads from the XKE payload thread would get queued together and reduce latency for loads/stores to RAM, or something like that.

It’s probably not very surprising to anyone reading this but CPUs often have “hidden” instructions, ones not defined by the instruction set architecture (ISA) but implemented by the CPU manufacturer. Sometimes these have a special instruction encoding and other times you’d use an existing instruction in a nonsensical way to tell the CPU to do a special operation.

In the case of PowerPC the ISA actually has some well defined instructions for changing the priority of a hardware thread by executing a special OR instruction with all 3 register operands set to the same specific register based on what priority you want the hardware thread to run at. For example:

or r1, r1, r1 # Low priority

or r2, r2, r2 # Medium priority

or r5, r5, r5 # High priority

The Xbox 360 SDK docs describe a few intrinsic macros that can be used to set the priority of the hardware thread the code is running on: __SetHWThreadPriorityLow, __SetHWThreadPriorityMed, and __SetHWThreadPriorityHigh. The actual CPU instructions used by these macros are slightly different than what I listed above (these macros are xenon CPU specific) but that doesn’t really matter.

The SDK docs describe every core as having 32 dispatch slots which are split evenly between hardware threads running at medium priority (which is the default priority). By using the __SetHWThreadPriorityLow and __SetHWThreadPriorityHigh intrinsic macros you can have one hardware thread use 31 of the 32 dispatch slots and the other only use 1. How the dispatch slots relate to number of instructions fed to the CPU execution units I’m not sure (again I have no idea how a CPU pipeline actually works), but being able to go from 16/16 to 1/31 sounds pretty handy for scheduling the exploit threads.

Using these intrinsic macros Máté was able to schedule the exploit threads such that the hardware thread running the XKE payload was only getting 1 of the 32 dispatch slots while the ciphertext overwrite thread got the remaining 31 slots. The result was that the CPU was now spending the overwhelming majority of time in the ciphertext detection loop than it was actually running the XKE payload.

Improved Ciphertext Overwrite Detection

The last improvement was something I came up with while working on the Peer Pressure exploit to try and make the Bad Update exploit as stable as I could get it. In the original PoC I had discovered the compressed bootloader data the XKE payload operates on was compressed into 15 blocks with all but the last block having a decompressed size of 0x8000 bytes. If the XKE payload attack was successful part of the last segment of the hypervisor would be overwritten with the decompressed data for one or more of the compressed blocks. By observing the ciphertext for the last segment of the hypervisor in two distinct locations I could determine if the last block of compressed data was written to it by the XKE payload.

The attack was setup such that if the last block of compressed data was written to the hypervisor at a specific offset it would change the instructions for one of hypervisor syscalls to a write-what-where primitive I could use to get full hypervisor code execution. However, there was a flaw in how the ciphertext was being observed which not only led to false positives that would crash the console but also missed iterations where the last block was written to memory successfully.

Above is the original implementation for the exploit thread that ran the XKE payload and checked for ciphertext changes in the last segment of the hypervisor. The lines relevant to ciphertext observation have been highlighted. Because the same thread is both running the XKE payload and checking for ciphertext changes it can only detect if the ciphertext has changed at all and not how many times it changed. Put more simply: I could only infer if one of the compressed blocks was written to memory, but not how many blocks were written. With that in mind lets run through two scenarios that could happen when running an iteration of the XKE payload while attempting to get compressed block 14 written to memory.

Missing Successful Writes

While running the XKE payload the race attack is successful on some block N such that N < 14 (0x8000 bytes get written) and successful on block 14 (less than 0x8000 bytes). Upon returning from HvxKeysExecute we observe the ciphertext for two locations in the target write zone and see that the ciphertext has changed in both locations. We can’t infer that block 14 was written after block N because we don’t have the ability to observe how many times the ciphertext changed. Thus we consider this a failed iteration even though it was successful.

False Positive Write

Assume we have just executed an iteration of the XKE payload that exhibits the missed successful write behavior for some block N and block 14. The last segment of the hypervisor now contains the data for block 14 and the tail data for some block N. We run another iteration of the XKE payload and this time only block N is written. When we observe the ciphertext changes for this iteration we’ll see the ciphertext at the first location has change but the ciphertext at the second location hasn’t because it already contained the ciphertext for the tail data of block N from the previous iteration.

This gets detected as a write for block 14 and the exploit will try to execute some hypervisor code assuming the instruction pattern for the target syscall has been changed to the write-what-where pattern found in bock 14. However, the instruction pattern is actually random instructions found in block N and will cause the console to crash.

The New Detection Method

Now that the cache flushing primitive was significantly improved it was possible to observe the ciphertext changes for each block of compressed data that was successfully written to the target region of hypervisor memory. The solution I came up with for the detecting if block 14 was written to memory was quite simple: I created a new thread that continuously watched the ciphertext for changes and counted how many changes were observed.

If the counter reached 15 once the XKE payload was done executing then we know all 15 blocks were written to memory and thus the last block had to have been written. If we observed anything less we simply consider it a failed iteration and try again. Here’s the code for the new ciphertext detection thread:

Too Much Pressure

The new ciphertext observation function worked great but there was a new problem it introduced. Due to the amount of pressure I was putting on CPU cache the console would crash about 30% of the time when executing the XKE payload. When the XKE payload runs it takes the compressed update data buffer and does an in-place relocation to move it from unprotected memory to protected memory so it can’t be tampered with asynchronously. After the XKE payload runs its main logic it’ll do another in-place relocation to move the update data back to unprotected memory before returning.

After modifying the XKE payload and inserting a bunch of printf calls I was able to determine that the console would crash in a function I called HvpRelocateProtectedToPhysical when trying to move the update data from protected memory back to unprotected memory. The function works by looping over a region of memory and for each CPU cache line worth of data (128 bytes) it will:

Read the entire cache line into CPU registers using the protected source address. Invalidate both data and instruction caches for the source address, zero the cache line for the destination address. Write the data back to memory using the unprotected destination address.

Here’s the disassembly for the inner loop of the HvpRelocateProtectedToPhysical function:

In the modified version of the XKE payload I added a bunch of printf calls in a re-implemented version of this function so I could monitor were it would crash:

After running a few dozen iterations I was able to determine that the CPU would crash when trying to write data back to the unprotected destination address on the line highlighted in red. As I mentioned earlier in the improved cache flushing section I made some modifications to Máté’s original implementation to put more pressure on cache which made the new ciphertext observation method more reliable.

I don’t know exactly what’s happening here that causes the CPU to crash when trying to write data back to the unprotected destination address. Perhaps one of the cache invalidation instructions didn’t fully complete before the store instruction was executed, or maybe there’s some edge case with respect to the custom memory pathways when the CPU is starved for cache. Regardless, I did manage to find a way to work around this issue.

Since the crash happens after we would have been able to observe all 15 blocks of data being written to hypervisor memory the solution I came up with was to immediately stop the cache flushing thread and drop the L2 locks once the ciphertext change counter hits 15. This reduces the pressure on CPU cache before the call to HvpRelocateProtectedToPhysical which prevents it from crashing. I moved the L2 cache locks into the ciphertext observation thread which we can see on line 5. Once we observe all 15 blocks of data have been written to memory we drop the L2 locks on line 36, and signal to the cache flushing thread to immediately terminate on line 40.

There’s still an edge case where we don’t observe all 15 blocks being written and thus won’t be able to reduce pressure on CPU cache before the call to HvpRelocateProtectedToPhysical. But this didn’t seem to matter. With all the improvements the exploit is usually successful in the first run of the XKE payload and at worst it may take 2-5 iterations, but I didn’t encounter any crashes when testing. It’s still possible it could happen but I think it’s very rare it does.

Conclusion

So there you have it, thanks to all the improvements from ihatecompvir, InvoxiPlayGames, and Máté the Bad Update exploit is now instantaneous and has nearly 100% success rate, and you only need to copy a few files to a USB stick to hack your console. When I released the original PoC I made some statements like “I don’t think this can be optimized any further” mostly to avoid endless comments from non-technical people spit balling random useless ideas. The truth is I always thought it could be optimized further but I didn’t expect it would ever reach the point it’s at now.

I think the biggest thing I learned here is that I should have taken a break after I completed the first iteration of Bad Update and came back with a clear mind to try and refine it. Having just found one of the only two bugs in the Xbox 360 hypervisor I put a lot of pressure on myself to get this exploit working at all. It took a lot of effort and sleepless days to pull it off and in the end I got tunnel vision chasing issues that didn’t really matter which distracted me from the real issues at hand. Had I taken a break after the initial PoC and came back a few weeks later I probably could have had something more refined for the initial release even if it wasn’t as refined as it is now.

Any ways, that does it for part 3. You can find the source code for the Bad Update improvements on my GitHub. Part 4 which covers the Peer Pressure exploit will be out soon so stay tuned for that!

item.title: Less Popular Than Coal
item.description:
Hi there, argmin readers! Today’s post is a late and brief reaction to a tiny subplot of yesterday’s historic election: the widespread rejection of AI datacenters. It was inspired by an insightful Dan Davies thread on bluesky that I have been unable to get out of my head.

Elections are a muddled measurement of “public opinion,” but they’re probably the only real measurement we get. And with every surprising measurement, a good rational agent must reflect on its beliefs. So what should we passive rational observers make of this historically large swing towards the Democratic Party in yesterday’s vote?

Obviously, this is a major repudiation of Donald Trump, his policies, and the Republican Party. However, you readers probably don’t come here for my political takes, and I don’t want to use this Substack for them anyway. Even if it wasn’t the biggest issue on the ballot, something closer to home is worth pondering. The American people are loud and clear that they hate AI.

Nearly fifty measures explicitly about building data centers appeared on ballots across the nation. All of them look like they will vote to limit further construction. A datacenter moratorium was part of Gina Hinojosa’s platform in her successful bid to become the first Democratic Party governor of Texas in over 30 years. The anti-datacenter position was undeniably the winning one. Poll results from this last summer showed people would rather have a coal plant in their backyard than a datacenter. Now elections confirm these sentiments were real.

We could try to convince ourselves that this sentiment is just about datacenters themselves. They are gross, gigantic buildings that employ no one, make a ton of noise, and are often powered with dirty energy. Who would want one of those? But datacenters are also a big, ugly, legible signal of a deeply unpopular industry.

At some point, we techy folks have to reckon with how much people hate what we build. We can point to revealed preferences all we want (people are adopting it! It’s making money!), but we did this during the social media boom of the 2010s (people spend a ton of time doomscrolling, therefore it’s good!). These economic numbers are also measurements, but we have to reconcile them with other data. Adoption and economic growth are so concentrated in so few hands that, while this props up our stock indices, it doesn’t lead to tangible benefits for everyone else.

Certainly, it doesn’t help that the industry has been selling itself as coming for everyone’s jobs. It doesn’t help that many prominent people working at these companies take to social media to gleefully exclaim that they think there’s more than a 10 percent chance that their company will kill everyone on earth. It doesn’t help that the big AI companies have been caught committing felonious cybercrimes all summer. It also doesn’t help that the leaders of these companies have been quite visibly embracing the Trump administration. Hugging a loser is a bad look, guys.

It’s a shame, because the technology is truly amazing. The AI true believers (accidentally) built something very cool that I would not have thought possible five years ago. But this amazing technology makes everyone miserable! It even immiserates its biggest boosters, who get sucked into productivity doom loops managing swarms of agents that speak in a unison chorus of Claudish. What’s our positive case here? The torment nexus of “superintelligence” ain’t it.

I have a lot of friends, colleagues, and alums who make a living building AI models. And I guess a bunch will be infinitely rich after the upcoming IPOs. But if you’re working for something more hated than the tobacco industry, maybe it’s way past time you stood up to your employer and demanded a better direction. And no, an open letter doesn’t count.

I’m not hopeful that this will happen. Ten years ago, I wrote a blog post shell-shocked by the election of Trump and disgusted with my industry. The cameo from Sam Altman explains a lot of my pessimism. I’ve been soul-searching for a decade. The leaders of the tech industry, instead of offering a positive vision and doing better, ended up sucking up to the new authoritarian government. They did it with pouting and feet dragging in 2016. They did it with their chests out in a celebratory embrace in 2024.

Our industry and field need a complete reboot. But that requires collective action. How do we fix it? What do we do next? I’d love to hear your thoughts on how the tech sector can clean up its image and make a positive, populist case for itself.

"Successful people create companies. More successful people create countries. The most successful people create religions."

In general, the big companies don't come from pivots, and I think this is most of the reason why.

item.title: Local privilege escalation vulnerabilities in Linux
item.description:
A thousand fewer paths to root

We've developed an autonomous vulnerability discovery, exploitation, and patching pipeline. In one run with our cyber model, it validated and generated patches for 948 local privilege escalation vulnerabilities in Linux at an API cost of $1.2 million.

Security research that once required a separate, sustained investigation for each finding can increasingly be run as a systematic process. This document explores one of our efforts in this area.

Vulnerability discovery is becoming easier to scale, but prioritization and validation remain operational bottlenecks. We built a prototype to look for security flaws in the Linux kernel inside a controlled research environment. Our prototype identified and analyzed 2,308 candidate Linux kernel findings, dynamically reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities, and produced 948 local privilege escalation (LPE) exploits that could allow an unprivileged local user to gain root access.

We used this evidence to prioritize vulnerabilities for reporting and developed candidate patches for maintainer review. Following guidance from the Linux kernel community, we began with critical vulnerabilities and are working with Patch the Planet partners on further reports and patches.

In June, as part of our Patch the Planet initiative, we shared that GPT‑5.5 Cyber had identified Linux kernel vulnerabilities and developed 24 local privilege escalation exploits to validate and report them. We expanded that work into a pipeline, powered by an upcoming cyber model, covering vulnerability discovery, dynamic validation, exploitability assessment, and patch generation. When it finished, human researchers reviewed the outputs and reported found vulnerabilities alongside patches.

Summary

Methodology

At a high level, our pipeline works as follows: first it identifies security-relevant parts of the Linux kernel, statically scans those audit targets for candidate findings, dynamically reproduces those findings in an isolated environment, creates a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit to demonstrate exploitability, generates patches, and finally a human security researcher reviews the results.

The output of the pipeline includes a root cause analysis, a minimal crashing proof-of-concept, a candidate patch, and a full exploit to assist human researchers in assessing the severity of the vulnerability and upstreaming the fixes.

Findings

In a run in mid-October 2026, our pipeline using an upcoming cyber model dynamically reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities and generated PoCs for 291 information leak vulnerabilities and 948 working local privilege escalation (LPE) exploits for a commonly used Linux distribution. The total run cost $1,213,430 in API credits, or $1,279 per LPE exploit.

The target virtual machines ran a stock desktop operating system, not a weakened target, under the same threat model used by cybersecurity competitions (e.g. Pwn2Own(opens in a new window), TyphoonPWN(opens in a new window)). Historically, Pwn2Own and TyphoonPWN offered a $20,000 and $70,000 bug bounty for Linux kernel LPE exploits. Applying those historical bounty amounts to the 948 exploits produces a hypothetical valuation of $18.9M—$66.3M, approximately 16x to 55x our pipeline’s cost.

On an adapted kernelCTF(opens in a new window) environment, which is a version of the Linux kernel with reduced attack surface, our pipeline obtained 25 information leak PoCs and 21 LPE exploits. For comparison, 26 confirmed 0-day LPE exploits have been accepted by kernelCTF in 2026 at the time of writing.

The campaign cost roughly $32,936 in API credits. If the 21 vulnerabilities were accepted by the program, it would lead to around a $1.5M bounty award, ~45x the scanning cost.

To the best of our knowledge, the agents in this pipeline discovered and used at least 10 novel Linux exploitation techniques.

Reflections

The Linux maintainers and security community are working hard to rapidly discover and fix vulnerabilities. Within 10 days while the scan was running, we observed over 100 Linux LPEs had been patched or had staging patches from other contributors, with ~300 more being publicly discussed.

Given the rate of vulnerability discovery by frontier models, we believe automated patch generation is essential to secure software at the pace required, and to limit the exploitation window. With human expert-guided iteration, we believe AI-generated patches can be functionally correct, aligned with existing coding styles, and robust to attack variants. This is an important area for further research.

More capable models are able to discover new vulnerabilities in existing code, often including ones that have been around longer and are more complex to identify. Our analysis pipeline using the newer cyber model in mid-October discovered >5x more novel LPEs than a GPT‑5.6 Sol run in July, despite three months of hardening between the scans.

Large, complex software projects likely require multiple rounds of scanning and fixing vulnerabilities to “bottom out” latent bugs. Ideally this process is repeated with each subsequent generation of frontier models. This applies to both proprietary and open source software.

For the near and medium term, having access to a low-privileged account on an operating system, that isn’t up-to-date on its latest available patches should be considered functionally equivalent to root access for a well-resourced threat actor. Defense in depth, using sandboxes and isolation approaches like Firecracker and gVisor are important for limiting the blast radius of exploited vulnerabilities.

Within the next few years, we believe that if there are vulnerabilities in a given software project, frontier models will likely be able to discover them and even less capable models may be able to develop exploits once disclosed. In a world of no unknown vulnerabilities, it will be critical to build and maintain high assurance software, especially core software such as operating systems, browsers, image parsing libraries, the TCP/IP stack, and more. Investing in training models to write secure code by default, minimizing attack surface by removing unnecessary features, and formal verification are promising areas of future research to effectively scale software security, in addition to finding and fixing existing vulnerabilities.

The Linux kernel underpins Android devices, cloud infrastructure, supercomputers, and other systems used by billions of people. With more than 40 million lines of code, the kernel exposes a broad attack surface through system calls, networking, filesystems, and device drivers. We chose Linux to study how effectively frontier models could find vulnerabilities and demonstrate their security impact in a codebase of this scale and importance.

The initial vulnerability discovery stage produced thousands of candidate findings, too many for security researchers to manually review and triage. The operational challenge of our vulnerability discovery pipeline was not discovery, but determining which findings could be reproduced, what security boundary they crossed, and which warranted the earliest maintainer attention.

The mission of OpenAI’s Cyber team is to help secure the software the world relies on. We report API costs for each stage to help researchers assess the resources needed to reproduce and extend this work. These costs reflect the models, target configurations, and workflow used in this evaluation. Our broader goal is to help defenders find and fix vulnerabilities, reducing the opportunities available to attackers and raising the cost for them to exploit software.

Finally, note that we focused on methodology and measuring model capability in this research, not cost. We expect that sufficient harness engineering could meaningfully reduce the cost at each stage; thus, the costs we report are more an upper bound.

Our vulnerability research prototype is a pipeline of five stages, which uses an upcoming cyber model at its core:

Vulnerability discovery: Agents identify security-relevant parts of the codebase and scan them for candidate findings.

Dynamic validation: Agents attempt to reproduce each candidate in an isolated environment and preserve runtime evidence. This step outputs the reproduced and validated vulnerabilities.

Exploitability assessment: Agents test whether validated vulnerabilities could enable information disclosure or local privilege escalation.

Patch generation: Agents generate patches that address each identified vulnerability.

Human review: Security researchers review the exploit, patch, and proposed severity before reporting to the maintainers.

At the end of the pipeline, the system bundles a root cause analysis, a minimal crashing proof-of-concept, a candidate patch, and a full exploit to assist human researchers in assessing the severity of the vulnerability and upstreaming the fixes.

Not every line of code in the Linux kernel is security-relevant. Our pipeline used a team of Scout agents to identify high-value audit targets, which were then passed to Analyst agents for vulnerability scanning.

Scout agents read through each folder and file and determine what targets to audit based on their reachability (reachable by low-privileged users) and security relevance.

This stage identified 5,034 audit targets, about 2.8 million lines of code, which is roughly 7% of the whole Linux kernel code base, significantly reducing the cost of the security audit when compared to a full codebase analysis. This step cost $3,426 in API credits.

Next, analyst agents analyzed each audit target and produced candidate findings using a workflow similar to that of the Codex Security plugin(opens in a new window). At a high level, the analyst agents read the assigned audit target’s code to understand how it works, identify its threat model, and look for vulnerabilities in it.

Within 12 hours, the analyst agents produced 2,308 candidate findings after deduplication. This stage cost $316,549 in API credits.

A candidate finding is not the same as a validated vulnerability. At this scale, manually investigating every report is impractical for our research team.

We therefore focused on validating findings that a) were reachable by a low-privileged user, b) required no special capabilities, and c) produced measurable evidence of memory corruption.

For each candidate, a triage agent generated a proof of concept and ran it in an isolated virtual machine running a Linux kernel with Kernel Address Sanitizer (KASAN). The agent observed both the program output and system console, then iteratively refined the proof of concept until it reproduced the reported behavior or exhausted the potential ways of triggering it.

Within 30 hours, our system reproduced 1724 vulnerabilities, ~74.7% of the 2,308 candidate findings. Static code review alone can be prone to false positives, so we were impressed by the accuracy of the analyst agents and the effectiveness of the triage agents in autonomously creating working proofs of concept for almost three quarters of the candidate findings.

Most remaining findings either required elevated privileges or failed to reproduce within the time budget because of difficult race conditions, specific trigger conditions (e.g., a required allocation failure at a specific line), or time-consuming validation (e.g., refcount wraparound). Only 3.1% reflected incorrect analysis by the model, where the reported vulnerability assumed an impossible condition.

The validation stage cost $73,330 in API credits in total. We observed that in our validation pipeline, which needed to generate a proof-of-concept to confirm if a candidate is a real vulnerability, this process was more expensive than making a recommendation based only on static analysis, and the costs of attempting to validate a true positive and false positive were similar. Thus removing false positives earlier in the pipeline makes the process meaningfully more cost-efficient.

Validation establishes that a vulnerability is real, but not how urgently it should be addressed. A vulnerability that could enable local privilege escalation, for example, warrants greater priority than one that could only cause a local denial of service. With 1,724 validated vulnerabilities, the next task was to identify the findings with the greatest potential security impact.

An initial screening agent reviewed each report, crash log, and relevant source code statically. It was deliberately permissive to avoid discarding potentially serious findings, while filtering out cases without a plausible exploitation path. This narrowed the results to 313 information leak candidates and 1,238 local privilege escalation candidates.

Exploit-development (ExploitDev) agents then tested those candidates in isolated virtual machines configured with the protections enabled by a standard Linux distribution, including Supervisor Mode Execution Prevention (SMEP), Supervisor Mode Access Prevention (SMAP), Kernel Address Space Layout Randomization (KASLR), and HARDENED_USERCOPY. This helped prevent unrealistic assessments that depended on protections being disabled.

The agents produced 291 proofs of concept for information leaks and 1,169 working local privilege escalation exploits that could give unprivileged local users root access.

We performed variant analysis and developed 948 distinct patches for the vulnerabilities behind those exploits. We use that number to determine the overall number of unique LPEs. Successful exploits cost an average of $359 in credits to develop. That makes it relatively inexpensive for defenders to test the exploitability of found vulnerabilities.

The initial vulnerability screening agent cost $44,194 in API credits. The exploitation stage cost $775,929 in API credits in total, $84,929 for processing information leak candidates and $691,000 for local privilege escalation candidates.

On average, processing a local-privilege escalation candidate ($558) was roughly two times more expensive than processing an information leak candidate ($271). This is because information leak PoCs were carried forward from the validation stage and required less modification to become usable in an exploit. On the other hand, developing an exploit from an LPE candidate required many extra steps such as exploitation strategy planning, identifying vulnerable objects to use, mitigation bypasses and more. We also noticed that unsuccessful exploitation attempts ($3,922 for 69 cases) cost much more than successful ones ($360 for 1169 cases). This was caused by a few hard-to-exploit vulnerabilities (e.g. race conditions). Defining a reasonable give-up condition, such as stopping the attempt after making no progress for one hour, would have reduced the cost of ExploitDev significantly.

For each validated vulnerability, the system also generates a patch. We provide the model with the relevant source code and prompt it with best practices in patch writing, such as performing static checks on the patch, following the software development practices used in nearby code, and performing variant analysis to make sure the patch is complete.

Following the Linux kernel community’s suggestion, we have already sent out hundreds of reports and patches for critical vulnerabilities and are working with Patch the Planet partners to gradually send out patches for the rest. This work is part of our broader Daybreak commitment to support open-source projects.

In this section we share learnings, reflections, and additional analysis from this research.

During this research, we observed the Linux maintainers moving quickly to fix vulnerabilities and protect users. The scan was performed on the latest Linux kernel in mid-October 2026. When the autonomous scan and manual analysis finished after 10 days, 61 LPEs had already been patched upstream, 43 had staging patches, and 299 were being reported and discussed publicly.

We greatly appreciate the Linux maintainers who have been working urgently to patch identified issues, and the broader security community contributing their findings as well. This collective response is what’s needed to secure the world’s software. The rapid rate of vulnerability disclosure and patching also emphasizes the criticality for users and companies to keep software up to date.

Takeaway: Automated triage should take the rapid patching cycle into account. Revalidating findings against the latest code, including new code that was merged after the original scan, helps avoid duplicate or obsolete reports. This focuses attention on unresolved vulnerabilities and gives maintainers evidence that they can act on without adding unnecessary review burden.

While we were developing the pipeline, in late July 2026, GPT‑5.6 Sol found and exploited 166 unique LPE vulnerabilities for an end-to-end $513,690 cost in API credits.

In the second scan, in mid-October 2026, the newer cyber model found and exploited 948 unique LPE vulnerabilities for an end-to-end $1,213,430 cost in API credits. For both campaigns, we scanned the latest Linux kernel master branch at the time.

Takeaway: Rescan previously audited code as model capabilities improve. A more capable model may uncover vulnerabilities that earlier models missed, even when using the same research harness.

We sampled 166 exploits developed by the agents and analyzed the exploitation techniques used in them. To the best of our knowledge, the agents used 10 new exploitation techniques in the sampled exploits. We shared the exploitation techniques with third-party kernel exploitation experts and the techniques were new to them as well.

Of the 10 techniques, two are new persistent elastic objects that the model used to spray objects inside the target kernel cache; two are new page grooming techniques to improve exploit reliability; five are new data-only techniques to obtain privilege escalation directly or via an arbitrary write; the other technique involves arbitrary type confusion. For safety reasons, we omit sharing the full technical details of these new exploitation techniques in this post.

Takeaway: Frontier models do not just pattern match known vulnerable code patterns or solely use known exploitation techniques; they demonstrate creativity and novel approaches.

An important part of our team’s mission is to measure the cost of finding and exploiting vulnerabilities and use that evidence to guide defensive investment. Our goal is to help defenders fix vulnerabilities before attackers can use them, and make it cost prohibitive for attackers to exploit software. Measuring exploitation costs helps us assess how that challenge changes as model capabilities improve. In this section, we compare our pipeline run’s cost with bug bounty program rewards for the vulnerabilities identified.

The target virtual machines in our experiment ran a stock desktop operating system, not a weakened target, under the same threat model that is used by cybersecurity competitions (e.g. Pwn2Own(opens in a new window), TyphoonPWN(opens in a new window)). Historically, Pwn2Own and TyphoonPWN offered bug bounties of $20,000 and $70,000, respectively for Linux kernel local privilege escalation exploits. Applying those historical bounty amounts to the 948 exploits produces a hypothetical valuation of $18.9M—$66.3M, approximately 16x to 55x our pipeline’s cost.

We also tested our pipeline against Google’s kernelCTF(opens in a new window) vulnerability reward program, which features a hardened Linux kernel with reduced attack surfaces as the target. We ran the pipeline on the latest version of the Linux kernel (incompatible with the SLAB_VIRTUAL mitigation in kernelCTF so we dropped it from the config) under kernelCTF’s environment and obtained 25 information leak proofs of concept and 21 local privilege escalation exploits. For comparison, 26 confirmed 0-day LPE exploits have been accepted by kernelCTF in 2026 at the time of writing. The whole campaign lasted 112 hours in total, costing roughly $32,936 in API credits, with vulnerability discovery accounting for 83.7% of the API cost. If the 21 vulnerabilities were accepted by the program, it would lead to around a $1.5M bounty award, approximately 45x the cost.

Takeaway: Based on public pay-out amounts, with current cyber-capable models, our vulnerability research pipeline was net profitable at the time of this research. Defenders should proactively analyze their software so that it becomes cost prohibitive for attackers to exploit.

During exploitability assessment, ExploitDev agents were given a vulnerability report and tasked with creating a fully functional exploit. Our pipeline marked a vulnerability as exploited if a root shell was successfully obtained. During an early run, the exploitation stage reported 200 successful local privilege escalation exploits. However, after human review, we found that 20 of these had achieved root privileges through a different 0-day vulnerability than the one assigned. This suggests that even successful exploitation by agents needs proper validation.

We subsequently tightened the task constraints and added an independent check confirming that each final exploit used its assigned vulnerability.

Takeaway: For autonomous security research, verify the path to a result in addition to verifying the result itself; isolation, monitoring, and independent checks are necessary controls.

Early in this research, we explored the design decision of whether to build heavy orchestration around the agent to improve its cyber capability. Our result suggested that stronger models require lighter orchestration and hand-holding. And the marginal improvement does not justify the maintenance cost. As a result, we decided to remove the heavy orchestration.

The experiment compared GPT‑5.5 Cyber and GPT‑5.6 Cyber. In our observation, GPT‑5.5 Cyber did not consistently identify when and how to apply existing Linux kernel exploitation techniques. We then assembled 103 techniques in a model-friendly format, made them available in the agent’s environment, and prompted the agent to use them. Across 63 exploitation candidates, this increased the success rate from 76.2% to 88.9%.

When we repeated this with GPT‑5.6 Cyber, the model was better able to find, select, and apply relevant techniques on its own. We removed the technique/skill orchestration and this lightly orchestrated GPT‑5.6 Cyber workflow outperformed the more heavily scaffolded GPT‑5.5 Cyber workflow. Adding back the additional technique layer for GPT‑5.6 Cyber provided only a marginal 1.5 percentage-point improvement.

Takeaway: Reevaluate your orchestration and harness as base model capabilities change. Scaffolding that materially improves one model generation may add little value for a stronger model and should be evaluated for the maintenance tradeoff.

Initially, when directly prompted to generate candidate patches, the model would create functionally correct patches that mitigate the proof of concept but occasionally introduce other issues: more code than necessary, introduced potential performance tradeoffs, deviated from coding conventions, or failed to examine related code for variants of the same vulnerability, leading to incomplete patches.

Additional instructions and iterations on the patch generation process improved the quality of patches, which suggests that with proper handling, it is possible for AI-generated security patches to be correct, minimal, and consistent with existing code conventions. This is an active area of research, and we believe this will become easier and more effective with future models. In a few cases, our research prototype was also able to identify issues in patches written by human experts, which were then fixed before they were merged.

Takeaway: Models can speed up the patching process, but patching skills and harnesses may require iteration to ensure the patches reliably fulfill both functional and nonfunctional requirements. Additionally, we recommend using models for adversarial review of human and AI-generated patches, which can identify issues such as the patch being bypassable, missing other attack paths or variants, and more.

In our kernelCTF run, besides the 21 Linux kernel 0-day exploits, our research prototype also found and exploited a QEMU TCG vulnerability. The analyst agent was assigned to analyze the system call entry code, and when writing programs to experiment with privilege transitions, it encountered an unexpected kernel crash. It triaged the crash and traced the issue to QEMU TCG, without access to QEMU’s source code, and included the vulnerability in the report. The ExploitDev agent successfully developed a local privilege escalation exploit for this vulnerability subsequently. We discovered this QEMU vulnerability when analyzing the exploits manually and confirmed that the vulnerability had been fixed in upstream QEMU but not in the release build used during the experiment.

Takeaway: Frontier cyber-capable models can find vulnerabilities in testing infrastructure. We recommend testing each part of the infrastructure before carrying out offensive vulnerability research. We have proactively tested our infrastructure, disclosing and patching many vulnerabilities in Kata, Moby/Docker, gVisor, and other projects.

Our goal is to turn increasing model capability into a lasting advantage for the people securing the Internet. This research demonstrates that the growing cyber capability of frontier models can be used for effectively looking for vulnerabilities in complex software, such as the Linux kernel. Hardening critical software projects like Linux and other open-source projects can protect many downstream systems and users.

Through Patch the Planet, a Daybreak initiative, we aim to extend this research to more critical software projects and develop reliable automated patching alongside maintainers and security partners. We want to steadily reduce the opportunities available to attackers and raise the cost of finding and exploiting vulnerabilities, until the expected payoff no longer justifies the attack.

Every generation of models should help us build software that the next generation finds harder to compromise. We will continue working towards building a secure Internet that anyone can joyfully build on.

item.title: Introducing Images 2.6
item.description:
We’re introducing Images 2.6 in ChatGPT, Codex, and the API, bringing your ideas to life faster. With this, you can bring motion to your images with GIFs — from animating a brand mascot or character to turning a product shot into an eye-catching loop. You can also create polished visuals faster and refine them with greater precision — keeping characters, products, and brand details consistent as you edit.

People around the world now create 4 billion images per week across ChatGPT, Codex, and the API. On average, that’s more than half a billion images created per day.

Images 2.6 generates images 50% faster than before. In the API, we offer GPT‑Image‑2.6 Flare and Sunburst for developers to choose from. When quality is set to low, Flare can generate images in as little as six seconds. For work that calls for greater detail and precision, GPT‑Image‑2.6 Sunburst brings higher-quality image generation and even greater image consistency across edits when quality is set to medium or high. Flare also improves layout quality for posters, product imagery, and other professional visuals.

For moments that call for motion, GIFs bring another dimension to your ideas. Marketers and creators can animate a brand mascot for a campaign, create reactions and memes for social media, or use animated storyboards to explore character movement before video production.

And you don’t need a polished design to get started — even a simple sketch can become an expressive, animated character for videos, games, and more.

From personal reactions to brand mascots and product visuals, GIFs give people and businesses a playful way to communicate. Town, a startup building an AI work assistant, used Images 2.6 in the API to explore how animated characters could bring more personality to everyday interactions at work.

With Images 2.6, developers get more control over how images are created, edited, and carried into the next stage of a project. Image markup, already available in ChatGPT, comes to the API so teams can pinpoint exactly where to make specific changes. SVG exports make designs ready to use across websites, apps, and print.

A new complexity parameter lets developers adjust how much planning the model does to meet a request, with lower settings suited to quick edits. Image quality controls visual detail and fidelity, while complexity guides how much goes into the scene.

For most editing tasks, we recommend low complexity for faster edits, paired with the image quality your workflow requires. For scenes with many elements or constraints, try medium or high complexity effort.
